Confining and redirecting optical or radio frequencies is facilitated by ripples formed in metal dipoles at dual metasurfaces by exploiting phase disparities, thereby inducing spatially localized current variations that produce ripples in the spectral density distributions of generated or modified electromagnetic fields. This principle has been primarily exploited to control frequency and direction for microwave or millimeter-wave ripples, and it requires relatively long periods compared to the wavelength. To integrate this technology into optical systems, it is essential to reduce the duration and dimensionality of the ripples and understand the underlying physics in detail. This work investigates how line ripples move and form at a dual metasurface and provides theoretical and experimental validation, including discussions on the optimal conditions for controlling optical ripples.

A key advantage of Collaborative Intelligent Systems ( CIS ) lies in their potential for large-scale, human-cyber physical collaborative learning, combining humans and robots in a seamless multi-agent workflow. CIS, which is based on AI-cognitive principles, enables the creation of adaptable and resilient systems that can learn and evolve in response to diverse, dynamic, and complex real-world situations. However, CIS architectures face challenges related to the integration of cognitive models, AI foundations, and collaborative components in a unified and scalable framework. This paper addresses those challenges by introducing a new CIS architecture, developing a model based on Artificial Intelligence and Cognitive Science fundamentals, and demonstrating its applicability through a practical example in the context of large-scale, collaborative learning between humans and robots. The proposed architecture offers a promising starting point for open-source software implementations that could accelerate the faster, low-cost design of CIS models for a variety of use cases.

A long-standing issue with measuring variability is that most measures fail to capture asymmetry, despite being unbiased estimators. To address this limitation, we suggest modifying the median absolute deviation by squaring the values, resulting in a squared average deviation around the median. This new measure not only accurately estimates variability for certain types of data but is also capable of addressing the issue of positive data, providing a distribution-free assessment of variability. Additionally, we provide mathematical justifications for its properties and reliable estimation through bias-corrected methods. Experimental findings demonstrate that this new measure performs well in the absence of any prior knowledge about the data.

The task of relation extraction aims to extract specific relationship data from written text.  To improve performance in this task, researchers suggest incorporating knowledge graph link prediction as an auxiliary task.  In their proposed method, features extracted from a sentence through language models are used to predict whether two entities should be connected by a given relation.  This auxiliary task is trained using a knowledge graph dataset such as Wikidata.  Results show that incorporating knowledge graph link prediction significantly boosts the performance of relation extraction models.  Additionally, researchers discover that their approach effectively mitigates false positive errors, specifically on difficult relations that are frequently misclassified as positive when they are actually negative.  An in-depth investigation of the proposed technique, along with accompanying code and data, is available at https://github.com/sealab-nlp/sem_bert.

The Analytical Perturbative Quark-Meson Model reverts back to the Quasi-perturbative KMRS model when the Higgs field's potential is in its superfluid state. By incorporating finite baryonic chemical potential and analyzing the N-dimensional Landau Free Energy for quarkonium, we determine its dissociation characteristics in a N=3, 4, and 5 dimensional space. Introducing an anisotropic momentum tensor with two distinct eigenvalues, we found that the GM1 quarkonium state experiences dissociation at slightly higher temperatures compared to the GM2 state. Furthermore, in the presence of finite baryonic chemical potential, the dissociation temperature for the GM1 and GM2 states increases by approximately 30% and 20% respectively. Incorporating quasi-particle Debye mass instead of zero Debye mass results in an order of magnitude increase in the anisotropic momentum tensor's irreducible part, thereby producing anisotropy in the momentum tensor and temperature below the critical value of approximately 150 MeV.

Tb3RuO7 exhibits alternative-bond spin-3/2 Ru chain behavior alongside property enhancements when doped with chlorine. We employed quantum Monte Carlo simulations to investigate the internal magnetic fields exerted by neighboring moments on the Ru chains in an undchlorinated instance of Tb3RuO7. The results indicate that the Ru chains experience a uniform internal magnetic field along their lengths due to the internal magnetic fields along their lengths due to the internal magnetic fields along their widths, however, exhibit disorder caused by the random fluctuations of the internal magnetic fields. This leads to a partial loss of long-range magnetic order within the system in an undchlorinated instance of Tb3RuO7. Conversely, instances with multiple valence electrons exhibited long-range magnetic order.

Our approach modulates periodic signals to produce significant activations within compact networks, facilitating accurate high-resolution image generation. By manipulating a network's parameters, we generate visualizations that reveal how activations propagate through layers and demonstrate the hierarchical structure within networks. In contrast to existing white and colored noise methods, our modulated periodic activations produce more consistent results and provide additional control over activation patterns by adjusting signal frequencies. This level of control enables us to develop a marker system, where specific markers indicate distinct activation behaviors, and we use this system to illustrate how activations behave in different network layers. We find that our modulated periodic activations produce high-quality images and understandings of how they propagate, while the additional control offers more insights into network operations. These advantages make our method a reliable choice for network visualization and exploring the dynamics within large networks.

Machine learning models can make predictions in scenarios where data varies due to differences in underlying conditions, or covariates. This phenomenon, known as covariate shift, occurs when training and testing data are not from the same distribution. Detecting and adjusting for covariate shift is crucial to ensure reliable inferences. While there have been successful cases using semi-supervised and generative modelling techniques to address this issue, these methods often rely on knowledge of the data's statistical characteristics or prior information. This research presents a novel approach using a new type of flexible model that leverages observational data to determine distribution changes, effectively addressing the challenge without requiring additional information. Experimental results on artificial and real-world projects illustrate the model's capability to adjust for covariate shift.

A comprehensive exploration of the geometric principles underlying deep learning models reveals how they function. Insights from differential geometry illuminate the training process, linking geometric concepts to popular deep learning methods. The study focuses on the geometric structures of neural networks, including chains, matrices, manifolds, and tensors, to provide a thorough geometric framework for deep learning models and unifying the underlying mathematical principles.

Elser's famous decomposition problem from 1991 poses the following query: given a lattice in n-dimensional space, can one divide a parallelotope into polyhedral regions via a series of cuts, where each cut consists of a hyperplane that intersects previously unvisited points? Researchers subsequently reinterpreted this problem as a convex optimization issue, where the unknown variable is the size of the resulting polyedral regions. The optimal solution to this problem corresponds to the volume of the lattice's fundamental domain, where the lattice is formed by integers under a linear transformation. The main obstacles to achieving an accurate solution involve identifying the boundaries of this domain and determining if they consist of straight lines. The latter condition is met in one dimension due to the lattice's periodic nature, but it is not the case in higher dimensions where corners form and require examination. Determining lattice minima – points that are closest to nearest neighbors – is crucial in addressing these challenges, as they mark potential corners of the domain's boundary. This paper discusses methods for identifying lattice minima and applying these minima to solve decomposition problems for certain lattices. Specifically, it provides explicit solutions for n-dimensional lattices of rank 2 based on the way they are formed from integers in two dimensions. The approaches outlined here can also be used to address decomposition problems for other types of lattices, where the challenge lies in identifying the lattice's fundamental domain.

A key strategy for extracting insights from complex neural networks lies in visualization methods, enabling researchers to effectively communicate network performance and biases. We've adapted the Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation (LWR) algorithm, originally designed for supervised tasks, to address the challenges of jet substructure subtagging in simulated top quark decays. By replacing traditional image-based features with quantifiable jet properties, we've created informative variables that complement existing ones and provide insight into the learning process of these networks, making it easier to create reliable, interpretable networks even in the most computationally intensive environments.

This research paper presents an exploration into a specific variation of r-related Stirling numbers of the second kind, which exhibits a simplified representation when expressed as a product of two factors. We also establish formulae for the associated generating functions and a recurrence relation governing these numbers, as well as provide explicit values for specific cases. Furthermore, the paper links this particular family of numbers to a corresponding class of objects that share the same name, specifically in the context of combinations with repetition. To achieve this connection, we first develop a simplified expression for the generating functions of the degenerate r-related Stirling numbers, which is achieved through the application of a structured framework for the objects in question, as described in a previous paper.

A comprehensive collection of crystal classes is represented by the strata groups, with an extensive catalog by Sharpe and Strunz providing the foundational information on crystal symmetry.  Among the extensive collection, double gray strata groups exhibit unique properties, such as multiple gray codes, and an in-depth analysis of their classification along with related single gray strata groups is presented in this work.  Utilizing a specialized framework, the formal descriptions of group symmetry are applied to determine the irreducible representations within each double gray crystal class.  Additionally, related work on single ordinary strata groups is also presented, with a combined output providing a comprehensive understanding of the related groups.

Momentum operators are explored in the context of intrinsically curved manifolds. It's established that for Killing vector fields representing these momentum operators, the manifolds are either flat or belong to specific categories: those with a compact structure and a constant sectional curvature of positive value, occurring in dimensions of 1, 3, or 7. Specific forms for these momentum operators and their associated Casimir operators are studied, particularly for the three-dimensional sphere S^3. Furthermore, it is demonstrated that the Lie algebra structure constants for S^3 relate proportionally to 2ℏ/R, where R represents the sphere's curvature radius, yielding countable energy and momentum spectrums for freely moving particles. A particle's geometric position in S^3 is described using a geodesic momentum operator-based approach, analogous to the classical method, employing Killing vector fields. Combined with the Noether theorem, the article identifies conserved quantities for S^3 and identifies rotational symmetry momentum operators as vanishing operators.

The Hubbard model's failure to achieve convergence with standard neural networks is attributed to the sign issue plaguing such methods. This challenge is particularly evident when analyzing the dispersion curves resulting from the model's predictions, as it causes the worst outcomes to be excessively magnified. We address this problem by implementing a complex-valued neural network, thus mitigating the sign issue. Compared to previous studies, our approach is distinguished by its use of a simpler and more intuitive method for updating parameters, as well as a more robust and efficient design. Moreover, we present results showing the dispersion curves obtained from our model have minimal errors, thus confirming the hypothesis that the dispersion relationship of a metal-semituctor interface has a specific, nonlinear pattern.

In low-energy composite Higgs models, Flavon-Higgs theories offer a straightforward explanation for the neutral components of the Higgs and $Z$ bosons originating from a complex flavon field, thereby avoiding potential conflicts with flavor physics. This flavon framework also facilitates natural feeble dark matter formation, and it provides a simple mechanism for generating the required flavon mass, thus not introducing extra parameters. Numerical analysis of the Flavon-Higgs theory is conducted to determine possible model variations that meet the dual goals of natural flavor conservation and adequate dark matter abundance. Additionally, we examine the Flavon-Higgs theory's compatibility with recent LHC searches for rare $Z$-boson decays.

The perceived intensity of virtual wind effects is influenced by the speed of moving objects within the vicinity, according to a phenomenon called perceptual retainer. This research delves into the perceptual retainer by means of a psychophysical experiment, examining its practical implications on user experience in VR applications. The study's results reveal that users tend to overestimate the wind speed when predicting the movement threshold of objects, implying a positive non-linear relationship between the wind speed and perceived prediction error. We utilize this insight to develop a predictive model, aiming to achieve accurate wind perception by forecasting a user's perceived speed based on visual cues and leveraging machine learning. The model is further enhanced by incorporating the user's specific bias, derived from their unique VR experience, to optimize performance. Experimental findings demonstrate that modeling the user's perceptual retainer through machine learning leads to enhanced realism, as predicted by a metric representing subjective error. The greatest improvement is observed when the user's personal characteristics are incorporated into the model, resulting in a 23% reduction of subjective error.

To assess various approaches to expanding language coverage, we introduce two novel Indian languages, Kannada and Telugu, to the widely used BigScience multilingual model, showcasing that with appropriate training data and parameters, high-quality language models can be developed for multiple unknown languages. We compare our results to those achieved with traditional language models, such as BERT and BART, on 8 languages, including English. Our findings support the use of unified models covering multiple languages, and suggest that models pre-trained on a broader range of languages can exhibit enhanced performance in certain tasks. We make our model and experiment setup available to the public to facilitate further research.

Recent high-resolution observations using VLA and CARMA telescopes have unveiled previously unseen aspects of a binary system known as L1551 1S. Researchers discovered two components, designated as North and South, connected by a strecker tail, suggesting they share material. A study leveraging N-body simulations revealed that the binary system's formation could be attributed to the breakdown of a rotating core containing three fragments, each corresponding to the initial disturbances in the core. When the system's total mass increased, the binary components emerged due to the core's dynamics and gravitational effects, ultimately resulting in a system resembling L1551 1S. Specifically, the North component formed first, followed by the South component, and the mass of the system peaked at approximately 11 solar masses when the core's mass reached 12 solar masses. It is proposed that the binary components deep within the core merged to form a single protostar, and their remaining mass was dispersed and manifesting as mass asymmetry in the system, potentially accounting for the mass disparity between the North and South components.

This research introduces the m-ar-k-fast AutoComponent Analysis (mar-k-FCA) approach, an innovative method for analyzing discrete data. It combines the principles of the Fast AutoEncoder and Autoencoder Component Analysis techniques to develop a more efficient FCA method. Empirical evaluations are performed using various real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate mar-k-FCA's superiority to existing methods in terms of accuracy and computational performance. The source code for mar-k-FCA is openly accessible on the GitHub platform.

This paper builds on existing research linking finite model theory and algebraic proof systems, specifically Choiceless Polynomial Time and Polynomial Calculus. We demonstrate that introducing parameterized quantifier structures in Choiceless Polynomial Time, allowing the analysis of distinguishing graphs, enables us to relate it to Polynomial Calculus with Arbitrary Degrees. This connection enables us to derive lower bounds for parameterized distinguishing graphs within Choiceless Polynomial Time, by utilizing lower bounds for Polynomial Calculus. The main contribution of this study is the establishment of a strict separation between Choiceless Polynomial Time and Polynomial Calculus, answering an open question previously posed by Ghoshal, Hirschfeld and Rahaman.

A subring collection in a ring $R$, that is associative, commutative nor unital, is defined as proper subrings set-theoretic union equating $R$. If such a collection can be chosen countably infinite, the ring is referred to as $\sigma$-ring. Furthermore, a ring is $\sigma$-elementary when it is $\sigma$-ring, commutative, and non-unital. Notably, until now there have been only two known instances of $\sigma$-elementary rings, specifically the integers modulo $32$, and the ring of $2\times 2$ matrices over the rational numbers. This research paper successfully identifies a new infinite family of $\sigma$-elementary rings.

Social media platforms play a crucial role in shaping public opinion, with vast amounts of information disseminated daily. Despite the vast quantity of data, social media algorithms streamline our feed, often presenting us with information on the most prominent stories. This makes social media an ideal setting for propagating unfalsifiable claims, as they cannot be disproven even with extensive evidence. Such claims are becoming increasingly common, with numerous examples involving the COVID-19 pandemic, conspiracy theories, and climate change denial. A recent study found that a high percentage of unfalsifiable claims online received significant levels of engagement and were often shared by influential individuals. A framework for distinguishing unfalsifiable claims has been proposed, consisting of three components: identifying claims that are inherently untestable, applying a standard to evaluate the evidence presented, and assessing the likelihood of manipulation. This framework aims to investigate the characteristics and dissemination of unfalsifiable claims, with a particular focus on those surrounding the COVID-19 pandemic and climate change.

This research proposes a novel approach for identifying incidents in real-time on social media. We have developed a device-independent algorithm that utilizes a dynamic decision matrix to determine incident detection thresholds based on quantifiable criteria related to post prevalence, spatial distribution, and temporal consistency. To ensure accuracy, we utilized data from Chicago, IL, to create a correlation matrix representing street segment relationships. We applied the Max-Weight matrix, which prioritizes physically connected segments, to guide incident detection. We tested various detection methods, including traditional techniques and more advanced approaches like clustering, in contrast to traditional methods on real-world data, and found that they outperformed others in accurately locating incidents and reducing false positives.

New, high-precision data from the cosmic microwave background lensing measurements and tomographic galaxy surveys in the upcoming years will enable more efficient cross-correlation analysis. We examine the advantages of employing the skewed lensing potential bispectrum, specifically its $X0X1$ component, due to its improved sensitivity to cosmological parameters compared to the conventional $XX$ bispectrum. We introduce an accelerated, fast polynomial transformation method for generating skewed bispectra, which generates all $X0X1$ components directly from the $XX$ bispectra without further computation. This technique can be applied to both numerical simulations and data, and we utilize it to investigate the $X0X1$ component in the CMB and lensing data from the Planck survey and the DESI galaxy survey. As a result, we find that the $X0X1$ component provides significantly more information about the neutrino mass, with an order of magnitude improvement in the signal-to-noise ratio compared to the conventional $XX$ component for a given set of data.

A critical issue in machine learning is the need for improved robustness against malicious manipulation.  We examine the problem of maintaining consistency in Bayesian inference when contingent risks are involved.  By introducing an innovative concept of robust probabilistic thresholds (RPTs), we define a reliable boundary for Bayesian inference outcomes.  RPTs offer two distinct advantages: first, they can be verified without access to the data, and second, they can be computed efficiently.  We establish a relationship between RPTs and adversarial norms such as $\ell_\infty$ norms, which allows us to construct verifiable robust thresholds.  This concept is further applied to well-known Bayesian inference methods, such as Bayesian regression, to enhance their adversarial robustness.  We demonstrate that models trained with these improved threshold bounds not only provide verifiable robustness but also yield superior performance in standard (non-robust) settings compared to conventional approaches.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors in the country. To address the pressing issue, this paper aims to investigate the propagation patterns of rumors and their impact on citizens during the pandemic in China. To attain this goal, an algorithm for identifying new rumors was developed and implemented to track 181 COVID-19 related rumors spread through social media platforms Weibo and Douyin. Analyzing the data showed that most rumors were spread quickly in the early stages of the pandemic and often received significant attention from users. Furthermore, our results indicated that people's reactions to rumors in the healthcare context were more intense than in other cases, and individuals sharing rumors were more likely to promote their spread than inhibitors. To measure the impact of rumors, a quantitative metric was proposed, reflecting their influence on users' behavior, the mental state of readers, and the pandemic spread. The analysis revealed that one quarter of all rumors had a significant impact on users in China, suggesting the necessity of timely and effective countermeasures to control the spread of rumors.

This study investigates the effects of hyperspectral dimensionality reduction on pixel classification tasks. We demonstrate that common methods, which aim to streamline hyperspectral images for easier processing, in fact compromise the accuracy of subsequent classifications. Hyperspectral images comprise numerous spectral bands that capture detailed substances within scenes, but reducing their spectral domain also eliminates this critical detail, we found. By employing a simple, effective, and open-source classification framework, we clearly illustrate the drawbacks of dimensionality reduction on pixel classification. Our research highlights the importance of accurately retaining the spectral structure of hyperspectral images to capture scene details and ensure accurate pixel classification results.

Recent advances in transformer-based language models have led to significant improvements in text compression. Researchers examining this phenomenon focus on the feasibility of using neural networks to compress text, but a key aspect is overlooked: whether the compressed output corresponds to the original input intent. This is crucial when working with sequences with hidden meanings and ambiguous baselines. This paper investigates the question of whether neural networks trained on text data can learn to compress sequences reliably while preserving their original meaning. It's a question akin to the Hall-Rogers problem, concerning the feasibility of solving the problem using a model that only sees individual tokens, not context. Our results indicate that authentic language models are capable of producing highly compressed text with preserved semantic properties, including analysis of the underlying distributions of text data. We also evaluated the output of a state-of-the-art language model, which achieved a compression ratio of 50% with preserved semantic accuracy, through both manual and automated assessments.

A novel prediction method, referred to as ProCS, enables fast and accurate prediction of key protein amide proton chemical shift values, yielding a precision of 0.4 parts per million with a 10-fold improvement over existing estimates. ProCS is comprised of three key components: a quantum mechanically driven framework for chemical shift prediction, a machine learning algorithm for shift prediction, and a profile-based scoring system that assesses the likelihood of resonances corresponding to specific protein structures. ProCS's precision and accuracy were validated through rigorous testing against experimental data for 42 distinct proteins, as well as through comparative analysis in ensemble-based protein structure prediction methods, including ROSETTA, Viper, and FFASPy. Results indicate ProCS surpasses other prediction methods in terms of precision and accuracy, while also offering significantly increased speed, with predictions capable of being generated 180 times faster than Viper's. Furthermore, ProCS was successfully applied to determine the three-dimensional structures of three experimentally verified proteins, allowing for the correction of errors in the predicted 3D models, thus highlighting ProCS's potential as a valuable tool in protein structure prediction and refinement.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is universally acknowledged as a key decision during model development.  Despite its significance, the impact of loss function selection remains poorly understood, with experiments often being used to make this choice.  This study investigates how loss functions influence deep learning models, with a focus on classification.  A comprehensive examination of twelve loss functions reveals their computational efficiency, ease of use, and adaptability to uncertain data conditions, in addition to their ability to control overfitting.  A systematic evaluation of the previously mentioned loss functions, coupled with an analysis of their relative robustness and layer-wise representation, provides insight into the best loss functions for specific tasks and applications.

Describing the behaviors of strongly correlated systems typically necessitates the use of advanced computational methods like the parquet theory to obtain accurate results. The parquet theory involves summing specific infinite series up to a particular order defined by the level of the approximation, x, which in turn necessitates the derivation of expressions for higher-order terms in terms of the frequencies of the system's components. Obtaining these expressions, also referred to as symbols, typically requires the application of non-rigid constructions like geometric transformations and the utilization of higher-dimensional auxiliary objects. In contrast, the authors propose an alternative approach to parquet theory based on a Hamiltonian framework, which involves representing the theory in a way that closely mirrors its standard mathematical formulation, thereby maintaining its mathematical integrity. This involves reinterpreting the symbols as matrix-like objects that represent the effects of higher-order processes. The authors demonstrate that, within the Hamiltonian framework, these matrix objects naturally become block-diagonal during the impurity approximation, facilitating the computation of physical properties through a simpler iterative method. The authors also show that this Hamiltonian approach can be extended to include effects of disorder, while maintaining the ability to obtain accurate symbols within the impurity approximation. The resulting approach is implemented in the MottKit software suite, which is used to compute the electrical conductivity of various systems. The results obtained from MottKit match the outcomes from a different parquet code, referred to as CL, MottGGA, or MottGW0.

The process of exciton condensation leads to the spontaneous creation of electron-hole pairs and triggers a phase transition in a semimetal that forms an excitonic insulator by creating a gap at the Fermi surface. This theoretical concept has been around for decades, but current approaches only offer approximate solutions; therefore, a reliable prediction of excitonic instability remains an open challenge. To address this issue, a new approach was developed that incorporates finite-temperature density functional theory with the constraint of self-consistent mean-field schemes as a starting point for exploring excitonic interactions. This new approach was used to examine $TiSe_2 $, a material that undergoes an excitonic transition at a relatively low temperature of about 400 K. Our analysis reveals that $TiSe_2 $ exhibits a strong tendency towards excitonic interaction and shows that the resulting gap is in agreement with experimental measurements. Importantly, this agreement provides confidence in the accuracy of our approach, making our framework an essential tool for investigating excitonic interactions in materials.

In the US, a variety of emergency services known as dispatch systems, often overlooked, play a vital role in responding to crises. They receive written reports from community members, including descriptions of incidents such as suspicious behavior or accidents, which are often highly descriptive and provide valuable insights into everyday life in the area. Researchers are interested in these interactions between dispatchers and community members due to their potential to offer a unique perspective on everyday events. However, challenges arise when attempting to analyze these reports due to their informal nature and the limited understanding they provide about the individuals involved. To overcome these obstacles, we propose a data processing framework that utilizes NLP techniques to extract key information from these reports, utilizing context to determine the relevant details to collect. By comparing various extraction methods, we identify the most effective one and demonstrate the potential for future studies to focus on incident-related data by incorporating relevant external knowledge.

To analyze the impact of Cooper pairs' spin, we applied the Ginzburg-Landau theory within the context of a nematic superconductor's context, focusing specifically on a d-wave superconductor. Under the presence of a non-parallel magnetic field and spin-orbit coupling, we found that when the Cooper pairs' momenta are not aligned with the magnetic field, a distinct paramagnetic effect arises due to the Cooper pairs' relative angular momentum. Furthermore, when the Cooper pairs' momenta are aligned, a unique paramagnetic effect emerges, attributed to the Cooper pairs' combined momentum and spin. By comparing our findings to existing experimental data, we observed that the measured upper critical field in the experiment was roughly 10% lower than our calculated values.

We introduce a key challenge in CL (concept learning) where the learner's ultimate goal is to demonstrate concept understanding via minimal evidence, but the learner isn't certain about when it has enough proof. A playful "provoker" regularly presents negative instances to confuse the learner and delay arrival at a confident conclusion. To tackle this issue, we develop MEL (minimax engaged learning), a robust method for addressing this learning issue, leveraging a classic game theory concept to find a suitable strategy. Our theory shows that MEL achieves nearly ideal performance when the provoker's tactics are limited, but can also handle more complex scenarios with an increasingly large number of provoker actions. Additionally, we provide simulation examples to illustrate MEL's performance under different provoker scenarios.

To study how music changed over time from the year 1600 to 2010, we measured the
variety of songs in several key areas using a measure called permutation entropy.
Our results show that music styles classified as classical, jazz, and rock have
distinct patterns in complexity and that music from the 19th and 20th centuries is
more chaotic than music from earlier periods. We found that music from the 20th and
21st centuries became increasingly chaotic until the year 1949 and then leveled off,
indicating that rock music was the most complex.

A novel category of stochastic processes that incorporate sequential elements and symmetric outcomes is introduced, where each state represents a set of outcomes. The proposed process builds upon a basic principle of reinforcement learning, incorporating a unique "click" action that advances to the next state or result. It's demonstrated that for processes with a fixed number of states or results, the long-term frequency of specific outcomes converges to probabilities that are proportional to their relative attractiveness. When the number of states or results is infinite, the long-term frequency of specific outcomes converges to a probability distribution that is consistent with a wide range of fundamental infinite processes, including random walks and rank-frequency relationships observed in natural languages. The study also examines the implications of multiple-click actions and the resulting control techniques for infinite processes.

We initiate a new direction in the directionless theory of computational ludics, by incorporating concepts from linear logic that drive the theory's progression forward. By introducing a balanced control mechanism, we develop a focused expression of the theory's core ideas, allowing for progression beyond the current model. Our work builds upon prior research, extending it with new insights into the theory's structured framework. The key innovations in this paper involve replacing the theory's original cut-based mechanism with a more fundamental role for focus, and developing a focused mechanism for managing control. The paper presents a focused interpretation of the theory, along with a focused normalization system for the lattice's lower part, and demonstrates the presence of a focused inversion map within this structure. The paper's findings are further illustrated through the examination of a simple example.

A prominent paradigm in reward learning utilizes human feedback via comparative evaluations, but their broader adoption is hindered by the expense and labor intensity of these comparisons. To overcome this limitation, we propose the Visually Aided Cluster Ranking algorithm, which leverages human feedback within groups to efficiently learn rewards. By grouping comparative evaluations and employing a proximity metric to identify patterns, VICR significantly reduces the required number of feedbacks needed to achieve a specified level of performance compared to other state-of-the-art methods.

We show that Smyth spaces are core-compact if and only if they have a strongest pre-order that is compatible with the topology, and in this case, the core-compactness can be equivalently stated as the condition that the topological space is generated by a collection of open subspaces that form a complete lattice. This result allows us to conclude that core-compact Smyth spaces are precisely those spaces whose topology can be described by a collection of open downsets. Furthermore, we demonstrate that core-compact Smyth spaces are identical to quasi-core-compact ordered spaces.

This study examines the creation and persistence of point vortex loops in ideal two-dimensional fluids, focusing on their inherent properties and behaviors. We demonstrate that point vortex loops are resilient and can be easily visualized using angular vortex patches, with their creation and interaction laws identical to those of traditional vortex loops. Furthermore, we develop a localized version of the Loitsiansky inequality, which helps us understand how a point vortex loop's velocity distribution changes over time and retains diurnal patterns even after disruption. We also investigate the role of a point vortex in a vortex loop's precession and find that its influence diminishes as the vortex moves further away. We derive closed-form equations for both the velocity and potential functions associated with a point vortex, which in turn allow us to calculate the pressure and evaluate the distance between two vortex loops. We then use these calculations to estimate the stability of vortex loops of various shapes and find that certain closed-loop configurations are stable while others are not. We derive a critical distance threshold below which two localized vortex loops will attract and merge, and also develop a method for calculating the time it takes for two vortex loops to interact and form a single, more stable vortex loop. We analyzed and validated our results through direct numerical simulations, and our research also includes detailed drawings of vortex loops in various shapes.

This study introduces a straightforward inference method using standardized augmented inverse probability weighting with predictions from machine learning models.  The technique is highly efficient, versatile, and easy to implement, making it accessible to a broad range of researchers across different fields.  We also provide clear, step-by-step guidance on modeling strategies and model assessment, along with recommendations for researchers who are new to machine learning.  The method's benefits and practical applications are illustrated through a series of realistic, concrete examples.

The role of $\tau$ is taking center stage in the current Higgs flavorportal scenario, where the natural size of the $\tau h$ interaction escapes theoretical constraints due to the large $\tau$ decay width masking the signal or because the $\tau$ sensitivity is relatively weak in tree-level particle physics processes. This article highlights the importance of $\tau$ physics, particularly in resolving these issues, and brings attention to the necessity of incorporating $\tau$ decays into the LHC theory community to accurately evaluate theory predictions' precision.

A tabletop-sized rotating annulus setup has been extensively studied to mimic the general circulation of mid-latitude atmospheric circulation. The device effectively replicates two crucial factors contributing to the formation of atmospheric waves: the influence of rotation and the interplay of temperature and pressure variations. The laboratory model enables researchers to control and analyze the emergence of waves resulting from these two factors. The experiment was conducted over a comprehensive range of parameters, with both the experimental and numerical models being comprehensive, and the results have been presented in detailed maps illustrating the wave patterns. The comparison between the experimental results and the simulations obtained from two different numerical models shows remarkable agreement, paving the way for the use of laboratory experiments as low-cost testing grounds for model testing and validation purposes.

A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. While this method has the advantage of using threshold-independent extreme value parameters, it comes with the challenge of parameter interdependence, making estimation more complicated. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the parameters of the Poisson process in a Bayesian framework, by transforming them using a tuning parameter'm'. This study develops a technique for selecting the optimal'm' value, which nearly orthogonalizes the parameters, by minimizing the correlation within their asymptotic posterior distributions. By choosing this optimal'm', the parameters converge faster and efficient sampling is possible using Markov Chain Monte Carlo methods. Finally, parameter values are then extracted through a straightforward transformation. We present results from simulations involving models of both identical and non-identical extreme rainfall in Cumbria, UK.

In the field of offline reinforcement learning, there's a critical problem to handle: dealing with the impact of maliciously crafted data. This issue is particularly pronounced in settings where the availability of high-quality data is limited and attackers can manipulate the training process to direct agents toward undesirable destinations. To combat this challenge, we're proposing an approach that not only protects against data corruption but also yields robust policies transferable to a range of environments. Specifically, our framework focused on Markov decision processes aims to find a robust policy offlining by minimizing the vulnerability of the learning model to corrupted data. This involves establishing correlation between the corruption risk and policy vulnerability, then formulating a convex optimization problem to find the most resilient policy. We also introduce an efficient algorithm for this optimization problem, providing theoretical guarantees, and conduct empirical evaluations that demonstrate our approach outperforms rival methods.

This study demonstrates the global logarithmic concavity of the cost function in the fast control scenario for a one-dimensional heat equation involving dynamic boundary conditions. Furthermore, it establishes the impulsive controllability of this system, which is characterized by the ability of impulsive controls to transform any initial state into a predetermined target state within a finite time period.

A consensus has not been established on the definition and optimal detection methods for out-of-distribution examples despite general agreement on their importance. We identified distinct behaviors of natural language models when encountering background-driven and data-driven discrepancies. Furthermore, a novel dataset and precise criteria for labeling unseen data as out-of-distribution have been developed. This research yields multiple substantial findings. Firstly, a refined understanding of out-of-distribution examples is obtained. Secondly, specific detection methods are isolated for background-driven and data-driven anomalies. Lastly, unusual cases that pose challenges for current methods are identified, suggesting areas for further improvement. Our work lays the groundwork for future studies on out-of-distribution examples. The collected dataset, along with our source code, are accessible at https://github.com/ChiaMinchen/OOD-types.

In recent years, self-assembled nanoachines have been gaining attention due to their potential for tackling biomedical issues. Among these machines, Brownian ratchet systems have emerged as prominent examples, utilized as inspiration or actual devices for converting random molecular movements into directed motion. Although theoretical models for these systems already exist, they primarily focus on thermal energy as the underlying source. This research delves into the possibility of utilizing inelastic electron tunneling as a means to power molecular engines. By utilizing a dynamical model based on Langevin's equations, we investigate the stability of steady states and their characteristics. Interestingly, when electric fields are present, the system can display periodic orbits. Furthermore, simulations demonstrate the system's ability to move in an asymmetrical geometry, mimicking ratchet-like behavior. Lastly, the influence of hydraulic pressure in an asymmetric barrier is explored, revealing the system's ability to display discrete, dissipative movement.

We introduce a novel property of transducers termed one-directional resynchronizability and establish it as a sufficient condition for both decodability and successfulness in the context of transducer algorithms. Unlike traditional resynchronizability, which is inherent to both sequential and transitive systems, our definition is tailored to address a specific limitation in current algorithmic methods. By defining different levels of one-directional resynchronizability, we demonstrate that they are all equivalent to a particular fragment of regular languages and, consequently, to context-free languages. Furthermore, we develop a iterative algorithm for constructing accurate non-deterministic automata from accurate transition functions, which reinforces a previously proposed method and serves as a counterexample refutation for a particular hypothesis surrounding successfulness in algorithmic solvability.

In inverse sampling with a Gaussian mean, the generalized convolution of two vectors modulo two needs to be calculated numerous times. This paper proposes an efficient algorithm to compute such generalized convolutions directly, surpassing the traditional O(n) brute force method. It also offers a new upper limit for the worst-case scenario, along with achievable lower limits for the best-case scenario performance.

The object GJ 229B, a T-dwarf companion to the low-mass star GJ 229A, has long been a source of confusion in defining the T-dwarf spectral type.  Recent spectral models of GJ 229B, produced using the PHOENIX code, revealed that the companion's spectrum, measured in the near-infrared, shows features that do not match its reported spectral type of T6.  Further research aimed to resolve the discrepancy between observed and modelled spectral data by applying the APOLLO code to reconstruct spectra of GJ 229B and its environment.  By utilizing the APOLLO code, researchers reconstructed the spectrum of GJ 229B from 0.5 to 2.5 $\mu$m and used the model to determine physical properties of the object, including its temperature, surface gravity, and metallicity.  Based on the new model spectra, the authors propose that GJ 229B has a temperature of 732 $\pm$ 16 K, a surface gravity of log(g) = 4.35 $\pm$ 0.03, and a metallicity of [Fe/H] = -0.20 $\pm$ 0.03.  Additionally, the model predicts that GJ 229B has a mass of 55 to 65 M_J and an absolute visual magnitude of 13.98 mag.  The research demonstrates the potential of the APOLLO code in resolving

To resolve the long-standing issue of fitting both $\pi\pi$ production and $\rho$ decays into the $e^+e^-$ spectrum near the J/$\psi$ mass, we explore a four-quark state with the quark content $[ud][ds]$ that couples strongly to both $\pi\pi$ and $\rho$ due to its near-threshold oscillation. When simplified into a molecular state, calculations indicate that a bound state could exist below 1 GeV, characterized by a mass of around 800 MeV with a width of approximately 300 MeV, primarily attributable to the $\rho$ decay. This potential state, if discovered, could be observed in experiments such as beam dump experiments or low-energy colliders where the $\rho$ vector meson can be effectively polarized.

We have refined our theoretical predictions for $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ generated by topological charm quark decays within the standard model. Our revised estimate for $\phi_s$ is $0.634^{+0.029}_{-0.030}$, resulting from a more precise calculation of $\delta_\phi^s$. Additionally, the impact of charm quark form factors on $\Delta\Gamma_s$ has been assessed, contributing approximately $3 \times 10^{-4}$ rad to the state's decay width. Consequently, the predicted value for $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ decreases to $0.634^{+0.030}_{-0.029}$ and $0.1093^{+0.0009}_{-0.0012}$, respectively. These improvements are anticipated to significantly enhance the sensitivity to possible beyond standard model interpretations of forthcoming $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ measurements from LHCb's Run 2 data, particularly at high $q^2$ values.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is quantifiable by a metric called $\Lambda$. This metric considers factors like viral load, exposure time, and air exchange rate. A well-mixed model assumptions underpin the calculation of this safety metric. Notably, eye contact and proximity less than one meter to others significantly increase the transmission risk. Our investigation discusses the limitations of the $\Lambda$ metric in capturing urban bus transmission dynamics. Specifically, we highlight how the rapid air mixing in buses may inaccurately represent longer urban bus exposure periods. Furthermore, the distillation of infection risk into a single numerical value may oversimplify the complex nature of this risk. This can lead to misleading public communications and a lack of actionable insights for bus safety upgrades.

This study explores the beta decay characteristics of $^{135,137}$Te. We establish a nuclear interaction combining $pd$ and $pp$ Knösen forces with an added finite range Gaussian component, which yields satisfactory results for both experiments and theoretical predictions. Effective field theory calculations reveal that nonsolar relativistic corrections significantly affect the beta-capture rate at low energies, necessitating these corrections for accurate decay width measurements. We also determine the shell-model properties of $^{135,137}$Te, focusing on the $^{135}$Te decay to $^{135}$I with a unique spin-parity of $1/2^-$ and a mean decay width of about 34 keV. Furthermore, we investigate the anticipated beta-delayed gamma-ray decay of $^{137}$Te, which is prophesied to emit a 41-keV $\gamma$-ray with 20% intensity alongside the primary proton emission. Comparison with experimental data shows good agreement, reinforcing the confidence in our theoretical framework.

Double Sided Auctions are versatile and widely used matching algorithms employed in various industries, including network routing, online advertising, and publishing. Their simplicity and lack of market-specific requirements make them suitable matches. However, double sided auctions fall short in guaranteeing fair and predictable prices in time-constrained applications. In contrast, this research presents FastDS, an implementation of double sided auctions optimized for speed and efficiency. FastDS integrates techniques from combinatorial double auction logic and priority-based matching to develop a double sided auction algorithm. Moreover, FastDS includes a novel validation mechanism that ensures the algorithm adheres to the principles of double sided auctions. Finally, the research showcases the results of fastds auctions conducted across multiple platforms and examines its performance.

We utilized heavy quark effective theory to describe heavy heavy mesons, specifically focusing on F-wave bottom mesons, and derived a general formula for their transition form factors. Further, by applying light quark effective theory to the light quark side of the meson, we calculated several decay widths for bottom mesons, such as $B^0 \to a_0^0(\rho^0)\pi^+$, $B^0 \to \eta(\eta')\pi^+$, and $B^0 \to \omega\pi^+$. Our calculations were performed both perturbatively and non-perturbatively using the QCD sum rule method, and the results were obtained for three different decay widths: $B^0 \to a_0^0(\rho^0)\pi^+$, $B^0 \to \eta(\eta')\pi^+$, and $B^0 \to \omega\pi^+$.

Markov decision processes (MDPs) with natural constraints often lead to convex subspaces within their action spaces. This research delves into exploring the intersection of convexity and nonexpansive shortening, a concept initially introduced by Giannakopoulos et al. for studying periodic MDP solutions. Unlike their approach, which relied on limit analyses, this study focuses on direct periodic decompositions using Bregman matrices. It establishes the relationship between nonexpansive shortening and a form of strong monotonicity, which unlike traditional notions, is relative to the specific geometry defined by Bregman divergence. This research further demonstrates that nonexpansive shortening leads to unique periodic MDP solutions and offers algorithmic solutions grounded in convex optimization. It also presents a set of natural criteria, exemplified by Markov decision processes based on Orlicz functions, that ensure Bregman matrices can define desirable solution properties for periodic MDPs.

We introduce the LANDO method, a kernel-based optimization technique that leverages Clarify, a robust dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) method, to develop informative structures while maintaining stability in the optimization process. Our approach significantly outperforms alternative methods in the kernel learning framework by rectifying the shortcomings of non-convex optimization and poorly-defined cost functions. The LANDO method's robust nature and capacity to generalizable are validated by applying them to simulated systems and data obtained from a linear cavity-coupled resonator as well as a non-linear optical system, with outstanding results demonstrated in both cases. The kernel LANDO method is highly efficient, yielding optimal results within a matter of seconds, even with a large number of data points.

Utilizing data from the chess.com online community, the intricacy and similarity of chess openings were measured, enabling a comprehensive evaluation of the complexity of the chess domain. Initial findings highlighted chess openings as a highly intricate system, characterized by numerous distinct strategies. Analysis of similarity among openings revealed that the top choices often cluster around popular moves at the starting of the game, while closer inspection showed sub-categories of openings developing a gradual pattern in their sequences. To assess the complexity of openings, statistical methods were applied to the frequency distributions of various opening sequences. Ultimately, the study's results were utilized to map the inner workings of chess openings, offering insights for exploring alternative pathways in chess and guiding the creation of chess-playing algorithms.

This research explores the possibility of using accretion-induced collapse in dead white dwarfs as a source of gravitational waves, specifically focusing on minor mergers involving millisecond pulsars. In a theoretical model, it's demonstrated how this type of event can occur, and it's estimated that such occurrences could happen around once a day within a specific range – the gravitational wave strain amplitude of h Kurul being between $10^{-19}$ and $10^{-17}$.  Furthermore, it's hypothesized that these occurrences will be linked to the existence of an accompanying GW pulsation signal, and that such signals will offer valuable insights into the fundamental characteristics of millisecond pulsars, including their mass and spin.  In fact, it's suggested that the GWS pulsar signal can provide more precise information than the radio signal, and that the most reliable fundamental data will come from a subset of pulsars known as the 'heavy pulsars', characterized by a mass of more than $2.78 M_{\odot}$.  It's noted that such data will be crucial for refining theoretical models of pulsar evolution.

This study generalizes Noether's First Theorem to functional differences and formulates corresponding equations of motion for arbitrary order Lagrangians. We derive an expression for conservation laws, which we then use to demonstrate a specific property of these laws in the context of Lagrangian mechanics. This leads to a proof of a theorem stating that conservation laws for Lagrangians of order n = 2 are symmetric polynomials of order 2n. Furthermore, this study derives a set of nonlinear conservation laws for mechanical systems with n = 3, 4.

This study introduces an innovative breakthrough in 3D shape retrieval technology, enabling the retrieval of 3D shapes via virtual drawing. Our innovative approach facilitates three modes of innovation: Firstly, it enables users to freely sketch 3D shapes in 3D space, allowing for accurate retrieval of similar shapes. Secondly, it provides a user-friendly interface for constructing 3D wires from real-world objects, enhancing retrieval efficiency. Lastly, we've developed a groundbreaking method for constructing 3D solid models from user drawings in 3D space, paving the way for more refined search methodologies.

HD80606b, a planet that passes directly in front of its host star, undergoes a daily change in its shadow as it orbits due to its highly eccentric path. This variation causes the planet's transit times to shift by about 0.3 days for each year passing, which means the current prediction will be off by about 0.5 days by the end of 2023. Recent studies using spacecraft and ground-based telescopes have allowed researchers to refine their understanding of this planet's movement. A new analysis combining observations from the Spitzer, Kepler, TESS, and K2 missions as well as the HIPPARCOS mission, has resulted in a new calculation for HD80606b's orbit, which has enabled researchers to predict exactly when the planet will pass in front of its host star at specific times in the future. Specifically, the study has updated transit times for the next five years and has given exact predictions for specific dates in 2023, 2024, and 2025. Furthermore, the analysis has given precise data on the length of HD80606b's orbit and its tilt relative to its host star's orbit. Additionally, the study has given exact predictions for specific dates in 2023, 2025, and 2027 when HD80606b will be at its farthest point from its host star and enter a new phase in its orbit where it will be losing heat at a steady rate instead of rapidly losing heat as it passes

We examine how a linear equation of state, p(\rho), affects isolated, massive, spherically symmetric, isentropic fluid collapse. By supplementing the Einstein equations with the barotropic equation, we derive conditions necessary for a collapse to occur and ultimately form a black hole. Assuming a smooth, high-density distribution, we analyze the behavior of the gravitational potential and the effective mass, and explore how both asymptotic properties and local characteristics influence the formation of a black hole from a collapse. Based on this analysis, we determine the feasibility of isentropic collapse to a black hole for various forms of a linear equation of state.

Using the Iyer-Wald formalism, we derive corrections to extreme black hole parameters, including mass and spin, in expansions of various gravitational theories, including Newtonian and Riemannian gravity. These corrections are presented in a comprehensive table and demonstrate that extreme black holes induce non-zero surface gravities, directly relating to the presence of spatial curvature on their surfaces. Furthermore, we identify a fundamental difference in how extremality constraints are maintained in extreme black holes, specifically involving the correction of mass and spin parameters.

A key aspect of successful motor learning is understanding the reasons behind an end effect, which occurs when a robot's movement varies in its final stages. To learn motor tasks efficiently, it is crucial to detect end effects promptly. Research on end effect detection is primarily driven by reduced efficiency penalties in robot movements, although it also has implications for safety as well as progress tracking in motor learning processes. The authors of this paper develop a new metric to identify end effects triggered by inertia, weight, and friction. This metric leverages a straightforward calculation using a robot's characteristics. The proposed metric successfully identifies end effects in simulation studies involving diverse models. The implemented metric has the potential to be adapted for real-world applications by incorporating experimental data. The integration of end effect detection metric in motor learning algorithms enables these algorithms to make informed decisions during motor learning processes. The authors' study offers a basis for further research on motor skill development that takes end effects into account.

The de Sitter group has a expanded symmetries within a certain gauge, known as vibrant Poincaré symmetry. This symmetry is used to generate a set of invariant fields in a de Sitter space, resulting in a novel generalization of the Poincaré algebra. This generalized algebra, called the vibrant Poincaré algebra, is applied to a de Sitter gravity theory and to a theory of massless and massive particles moving along a de Sitter geodesic. A new action, called the vibrant Poincaré action, is derived for a massless particle, showing its equivalence to the standard de Sitter action, and a new action, called the pseudo-Poincaré action, is derived for a massive particle. Its action, called the vibrant action, is derived for a massive particle with a given mass. Additionally, a new action, called the pseudo-Poincaré action, is derived for a massive particle when its mass is arbitrarily large.

Upward planarity, a graph format where edges are drawn with start and end points ranked accordingly, is examined through parameterized methods in this study. Specifically, we develop new strategies for identifying whether a graph can be represented in upward planar layout, based on specific graph structure metrics. These techniques yield more efficient algorithmic solutions than before, for certain graph properties. For instance, we found that bounded treed width graphs, planar graphs, and k-outerplanar graphs can all be assessed for upward planarity in linear time. However, we also discovered that general planar graphs and k-layer planar graphs can only be determined for linear time if a specific parameter is known in advance. Additionally, we found that bounded treed width graphs, planar graphs, and k-outerplanar graphs can all be represented in upward planar layout in linear time as well.

Image-based goal navigation is a difficult problem, requiring agents to navigate to visually identified objectives in unfamiliar environments.
Previous methods often employ diverse memory mechanisms to track navigation history but fail to account for the fraction of relevant memories in their storage systems.
We propose the MemoNav, a simple memory-based navigation system, designed to improve the effectiveness of memory-based navigation approaches by choosing the most relevant memories to incorporate into the memory system.
To achieve this, we introduce a new metric called the memory relevance score (MRS), which estimates the likelihood of a memory being relevant to the navigation task.
Based on the MRS, we develop two memo-selection methods: the top-M candidates method and the continuous integration method, to enhance the performance of memory-based navigation in various scenarios.
Experimental results show that our proposed methods achieve state-of-the-art performance on the AI2-THOR benchmark, outperforming current navigation techniques by 50% to 10% in terms of success rate.
Additionally, our continuous integration method was found to be more efficient and flexible than other approaches, with a time complexity of O(N) and a mean extra time cost of 2.3%.

Heterogeneous wireless networks with high data rates are achieving great success, and this trend is expected to continue into the future. To meet the growing demands of users, in this article, we explore the development, advancements, and prospects of small cell networks from 4G to 6G. First, we provide a comprehensive overview of past, present, and future technologies, highlighting key areas such as LTE-advanced, 5G, and future generations of wireless communication. Next, we examine the challenges associated with deploying small cell networks in real-world settings, and propose potential solutions for addressing these issues. The article also delves into emerging technologies such as millimeter wave, terahertz spectrum, and nonorthogonal networking techniques, and discusses their anticipated roles in future small cell networks. Finally, we identify crucial research areas and propose future directions for investigation.

This overview covers various approaches to studying dynamical systems that are connected to networks. The work discussed draws heavily from two books "Dynamical Systems on Networks" and "Search in Networks", both authored by Janos Plosztosi.

We examine the relationship between operator growth and holography in quantum systems. In particular, we investigate how rapid growth of operators affects their contributions to the OPE seriers in specific contexts. Initially, we explore how operator growth impacts the OPE coefficients for a free scalar field in higher dimensions. We find that at initial stages, lower-order operators play a significant role in the OPE series. Additionally, we extend our analysis to the AdS/BCFT correspondence, focusing on the growth of operators and their connection to bulk operators in AdS spaces. Our analysis also encompasses fast-growing operators, including logarithmic operators that emerge in certain BCFT scenarios.

Researchers focusing on the Hoyle state, a unique nuclear structure, have found it difficult to agree on its decay properties. Recent experiments utilizing beam-rejection techniques enabled researchers to isolate a significant portion of the Hoyle state's direct decay component, which is almost unaffected by intermediate nuclei. By employing a novel Time Projection Chamber in conjunction with a Particle Identifier, researchers were able to identify 4He particles resulting from the Hoyle state's decay into 8Li* without relying on intermediate nuclei. Their findings support earlier findings by S* shells and contradict earlier conclusions by Chowder and others.

Significant breakthroughs are made when miniature electronic devices based on single-crystal silicon microcircuits are successfully implemented in practical applications. However, as engineers strive to replicate this level of success through the fabrication of miniature devices in other materials, they need to understand how stress develops at the microscopic level in materials prone to cracking. To tackle this challenge, researchers have explored the inherent length and time scales inherent to materials, which influence fracture instability. They have conducted in-depth numerical simulations to examine how these scales impact dynamic fracture instability, specifically types known as oscillatory and tip-splitting instabilities in two-dimensional settings. The results of these experiments provide valuable insights into the inherent length and time scales necessary for the practical application of miniature electronics based on single-crystal materials.

We examine the capacity and optimal power allocation of a link with feedback in a deterministic environment, where the transmitter has access to accurate information about the channel conditions. The link is represented by a set of deterministic equations, where the receiver's discrete nature is taken into consideration. The transmitter is given a power constraint and has access to feedback from the receiver, enabling it to adapt its transmission strategy. The goal is to find the best way to send information efficiently, given these limitations. To achieve this, we study a variational problem that involves finding the optimal distribution of information when sent through the link, and derive a solution by applying the principles of suboptimality and duality. The result shows that with enough available power, taking feedback into account does not reduce capacity. When power is limited, however, the channel becomes more noisy, leading to a capacity loss. The result is validated through a comparison with the case where only a binary link is possible. The knowledge the transmitter has about the channel conditions does not affect it, as this information does not provide any additional opportunities. The same power allocation strategy is shown to be optimal in this context as well. The achieved capacity is shown to be attainable through a scheme that involves sending information in a predictable, repetitive pattern. The same pattern is sent both ways on the link, where the transmitter adjusts it based on the channel's characteristics and available power. The result achieved represents an extension of previous work on the study of links without feedback, where a similar pattern was

A novel topological superfluid is introduced, characterized by related spin-singlet paired and Rashba-symmetry broken phases in the Rashba Hubbard model with attractive interactions. Employing a computational approach based on the finite difference method for the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model equivalent and the sign problem, the phase diagram and superfluid spectrum are computed. We find that a particular superfluid phase exhibits topological properties, marked by an energy gap in the spectrum and a non-zero Chern number, indicating the presence of fractional superfluid vortices. This topologically non-trivial superfluid phase is unstable and transitions into a supersolid phase with a crystalline structure in the presence of a periodic potential.

This study focuses on understanding tables within academic papers by deciphering their purpose, composition, and data to extract relevant facts and support them with table data. Our initial challenge, SEM-TAB-Facts, necessitated the accurate recognition of tables in scientific papers, their semantic interpretation, and the extraction of facts and supporting evidence in tabular form. A additional phase required the classification of tables based on their content to determine whether the facts presented were in line with existing knowledge or represented new insights. Our analysis revealed that teams faced difficulties in identifying tables, interpreting their content, and distinguishing verifiable from novel information. In particular, identifying empty cells and disregarding irrelevant data proved challenging for many systems. A review of the submission outcomes and system performances is offered below.

This analysis explores the essential role of noncommuting quantities in quantum mechanics, demonstrating that their failure to commute is not solely responsible for the complexities of quantum theory. In fact, a new finding indicates that commuting operators can exhibit complicated relationships even in the absence of particles. A theoretical framework has been developed, providing a clearer understanding of noncommutativity and its implications for measurement outcomes in quantum mechanics.

A graph G's metric dimension is the minimum number of vertices that pinpoint every other vertex using the minimum distance between vertices. A subgraph of G's "n-tim trimmed metric dimension" is the minimum cardinality set of vertices that pinpoint every other vertex in the subgraph, using the minimum distance between vertices, where the distance between two vertices is at most n. A graph G's trimmed metric dimension is the special "1-tim" subgraph's metric dimension. A new efficient algorithm for calculating the trimmed metric dimension of a given graph, for any given trim number, is described. This algorithm runs in O(2^k n ^((k-1))(1+log(n))/k) time, where k is the number of groups the graph is divided into, n is the number of vertices, and l is an upper bound for the distance between vertices. Additionally, an algorithm for calculating the trimmed metric dimension of a given graph's subgraph obtained by removing a set of vertices from the original graph, for any given trim number, is described. This algorithm runs in O(2^k m ^((k-1))(1+log(n))/k) time, where k is the number of groups the graph is divided into, m is the number of vertices in the removed set, n is the number of vertices in the original graph, and l is an upper bound for the distance between vertices.

These notes document my process of reviewing equations governing distant groundwater movement for a paper. By "distant," I'm referring to grounds several to tens of thousands of feet below the Earth's surface. Darcy's Law and the equation for conservation of mass are the fundamental equations needed to model this phenomenon. Darcy's Law describes water movement in a fracture or pore, while the equation for conservation of mass accounts for changes in water's energy and movement over time. These equations are non-linear due to factors like friction and port constraints, leading to complex solutions. Developing numerical approaches requires careful consideration to ensure accuracy, given these challenging equations. To tackle this issue, I reviewed existing simplification methods, focusing on cases where small parameters could be disregarded, albeit approximately. These parameters include very slow flow velocities, low fluid pressures, and highly permeable rocks. When these conditions prevail, groundwater movement is often near hydrodynamic equilibrium, allowing for simplified equations like those describing two-dimensional radial flow. While these simplifications work well, they may not apply to all scenarios, and when they don't, more complex approaches like finite difference, finite element, and finite volume methods are necessary.

This work has investigated the potential of integrating an ozone O3 and ultraviolet (UV) light system into a flue gas cleaning system, specifically designed to remove polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon emissions in the low temperature flue gas produced by municipal solid waste incinerators. Research has been conducted on the light absorption coefficients of gaseous O3 and NO2, as well as the absorption spectra of SO2 in the far UV range. This information has been used to model and optimize the performance of an UV-O3 system in a reactor, given certain constraints. Compared to an O3 system alone, the addition of UV light increased the reaction rate by as much as 180 times, effectively removing 95% of sulfur dioxide particles. To achieve the same level of reaction efficiency, the energy required was reduced by almost 90%. A numerical model of the UV-O3 system has been developed and validated against experimental data from a small-scale installation. The capacity to remove sulfur dioxide particles was again the key factor in this validation process. The models and results suggest that the combination of an ozone and UV light system offers a highly effective and energy-efficient solution for cleaning municipal solid waste incinerators' flue gas emissions.

As next-generation computing systems, neuromorphic architectures stand out for their energy-efficient parallel processing capabilities. To accelerate the development of neuromorphic hardware and software, researchers need accessible platforms for testing and refining their designs. While available simulation tools offer valuable analytical capabilities, they often come with steep computational costs. This paper proposes a novel virtual platform based on SystemC, designed to efficiently simulate neuromorphic architectures in multi-core CPU environments. By distributing simulation tasks among CPU cores, our virtual platform significantly improves simulation speed, achieving a notable acceleration ratio of over 30x compared to traditional sequential-based approaches.

Machine learning models known as argumentation frameworks, which utilize pairs of individuals to represent conflicts and relationships, are utilized in various applications such as ethics, medicine, and computing.  The framework's semantics is established by identifying the possible combinations of labels that can be applied to the individuals involved.  The concept of conflict-free sets provides a basis for the models and is related to other combinatorial entities.  Existing machine learning methods, which adapt the models to make predictions based on data-driven insights, are limited in their ability to address issues related to labeling ambiguity and uncertainty.  The framework of indecision forests is proposed to address these challenges by utilizing a distribution-based approach to represent predictive distributions as collections of labelings that meet specified criteria.  The model's ability to capture uncertainty is tied to the idea of "wallman semiotics," which involves collections of labelings that can be applied to the individuals involved.
