The Dynamic Time Warping distance measure is widely used to compare time series data, but its efficiency comes at the cost of a high computational complexity of O(N^2), making it impractical for large datasets. To mitigate this issue, PrunedDTW enjoys a sublinear complexity of O(NM) thanks to early discarding of unfeasible alignments, where M is the warping window size. However, this advantage is only effectively harnessed in similarity searches once a query time series is given, delaying the utilization of pruned DTW's property on preprocessed data. To overcome this limitation, we present EDPD, an early discarding variant of PrunedDTW applicable to precomputed distance tables prior to a similarity search, enjoying a sublinear complexity of O(NM). EDPD achieves this through the introduction of two novel bounds, making it compatible with both linear and nonlinear constraints, including a special case for unwarped sequences with reduced memory requirements. EDPD outperforms state-of-the-art methods on real-world datasets, encompassing stock price series with varying lengths, by means of exhaustive experimentation.

Current educational tools in software testing can either guide students towards correct answers or inform students of incorrect results without guidance. A new learning system is proposed that mimics the inquiry-based learning method by providing conceptual feedback when test results are incorrect, directing students towards relevant learning materials. An empirical study compared this new approach with traditional feedback methods. The study analyzed the impact of conceptually-based feedback versus two other methods - revealing test cases or providing detailed results - on students' performance in a software testing course. The study analyzed how these forms of feedback affected demonstration grades, course evaluations, and student interaction with course materials. The analysis found a significant improvement in demonstration grades when conceptually-based feedback was used, and also discovered that this approach decreased reliance on external help and promoted student engagement with course materials. Consequently, it is recommended that educational tools adopt the conceptually-based feedback mechanism to support inquiry-based learning.

In domains requiring reliability or transparency, explainable AI is increasingly becoming essential for handling deep neural networks. This study bridges the gap between existing approaches to NLP and explainable AI for deep learning, introducing a new invention: Explainer. The Explainer utilizes concept analysis and answer set programming to provide verifiable, detailed explanations for neural networks classified as binary, multi-class, or multi-label. The effectiveness of the Explainer is demonstrated through successful applications to four diverse datasets and its outperformance over existing solutions in terms of accuracy and user satisfaction rates. Furthermore, the research presents a timeline highlighting the advancement of explainable AI, emphasizing its promising potential for future research and implementation.

Graph Convolutional Networks (GCNs) have emerged as highly effective and efficient neural network architectures for handling graph-based datasets. Despite their success, particularly in node classification tasks, the graph structure's influence on learning has not been thoroughly examined. This study bridges that gap by investigating how the graph structure impacts GCN performance and reveals an unexpected yet significant finding: GCNs can exhibit an 'over-blurring' effect when processing highly organized graphs, resulting in superior performance relative to Residual Graph Neural Networks (R-GCNs), which demonstrate superior results on datasets with less clear graph structures. Notably, the 'over-blurring' effect is found to primarily influence the GCN's last layer, allowing researchers to enhance R-GCN performance by simply converting it to a GCN. This discovery offers valuable insights for future R-GCN improvements and challenges the conventional assumption that larger models necessarily achieve higher accuracy, prompting further exploration into the role of model scale in machine learning.

Dark matter particle production in association with a Z boson, which decays into electrons or muons, is investigated in collisions of proton pairs. The data, amounting to 137 fb^-1, were recorded at a 13 TeV center-of-mass energy by the CMS experiment between 2016 and 2018 at a series of LHC runs. The focus is on a pair-produced dark matter particles that each decay into a Higgs boson and a quark, resulting in a Z boson and three quarks that allow for the detection of a Z boson and up to three hadronically interacting particles. Relying on electron and muon separation, particle identification, and other relevant criteria, events are categorized as having either one, two, or three candidate particles. Events are analyzed using both isolated particles and broader hadronic scuts, providing two signal regions in total. Relying on razor variables, events are further divided into further signal regions. The analysis uses a control region defined by Z boson candidate mass and transverse momentum, as well as the absence of muons, to determine the background. The search reveals an excess of events over the predicted background, amounting to 2.4 standard deviations. Considering signal cross-sections, assuming a conserved momentum, the study sets a limit on the dark matter particle production cross-section in a specific mass range, ranging from 30 to 400 GeV, at 0.16 fb or

We propose two new distribution functions, each dependent on $k_\perp$, in addition to the D0s and $\chi_c$ mesons.  The first, the $P_\perp^{\rm D0s}$ function, tracks D0s mesons as they transition between being on and off shell.  The second, the $P_\perp^{\rm D0s}$ function, tracks D0s mesons that are on shell.  Both functions are supplemented by a third, the $\mathcal{P}_\perp^{\rm D0s}$ function, which tracks D0s mesons that are on shell.  Similarly, we define two new functions to track $\chi_c$ mesons: the $P_\perp^{\rm \chi_c}$ and $\mathcal{P}_\perp^{\rm \chi_c}$ functions.  We show that the D0s meson's quasi-particle distribution function is related to its particle-like distribution function by a solution to the Bjorken-like equation.  Conversely, we show that the $\chi_c$ meson's quasi-particle distribution function is related to its particle-like distribution function by a solution to the evolution equation for the probability density of a state with a given energy. Given a locally compact topological group G, we investigate the properties of spaces equipped with G-like topologies that are nearly continuous in nature. Specifically, a diagram of spaces and G-map morphisms can be extended to a long sequence of continuous G-maps with specific linear continuity properties. This extension is significant because it allows us to classify the topological properties of spaces having G-like topologies that are continuous in nature. Additionally, we apply these results to study the topological properties of spaces having G-like topologies that have a specific mean value condition.

Research into epitaxial relationships between films and substrates is highly active, driven by potential for cost-efficient synthesis of semiconducting films with precise composition and structure. However, achieving accurate epitaxy on aberrant substrates poses significant challenges. This study investigates the variation in epitaxial relationships between La$_{0.85}$Pt$_{0.15}$Fe$_{0.75}$Si$_{0.25}$ film and different substrates, consisting of graphene on sapphire with distinct surface orientations. By controlling chemical potential and temperature, the study changes epitaxial relationships remotely, achieving the first instance of a film growing epitaxially on a monolayer graphene substrate and also establishes conditions for film growth via van der Waals epitaxy, providing crucial insights towards understanding mechanisms behind epitaxial relationships and film growth phenomena.

We analyze how to make reliable forecasts for key statistics in multivariate time series data that exhibit heavy-tailed behavior, even when the underlying model isn't completely specified. We propose a method that utilizes a particular type of model, incorporating non-fixed components to account for the unique characteristics of individual time series, while also making allowances for similarities among them. This model builds upon the existing 'common components and errors' (CCE) model, originally developed for normally distributed data, and adapts it for use with multivariate time series that exhibit heavy-tails. We demonstrate that parameter estimates remain reliable under more flexible assumptions, and also provide confidence intervals for key statistics, as well as forecast error probabilities. The methodology is supported through simulations and applied to real-world analysis of two well-known financial market indices.

JWST has identified multiple trusted photometric redshift estimates for over 68,000 galaxies across five redshift ranges, with one particularly notable object: a galaxy located at a redshift of 0.87 in the massive galaxy cluster ACT-CL J0102-4915, appearing to be distorted by the cluster's gravitational field and featuring multiple images. Analyzing this system, known as CSW0304-495, JWST spectra reveal three components, each corresponding to a different redshift: 0.87, 1.38, and 1.54. By incorporating these findings into existing models, scientists propose a new lens model for ACT-CL J0102-495 and use it to study the system's dynamics, concluding that the galaxy underwent significant star formation between the ages of 1 and 3 billion years. Furthermore, the model estimates that the cluster's core is home to over 4300 red supergiant stars, an upper limit that may be as high as 20% of the total stellar mass in this region. JWST data for another massive galaxy cluster, EL 0959-2133, also reveal insistent indications of a red supergiant star population in its core, supporting the hypothesis that these stars could play a crucial role in shaping the galaxy's chemistry and appearance.

The rising demand for online content streaming has led ISPs to struggle with the ability to meet the demands of their subscribers, resulting in poor network quality during peak hours. To address this, ISPs are developing Business-to-Business models, where they partner with content providers to guarantee quality of service for their subscribers. This paper discusses the challenges of profit distribution between these partners, proposing a new scheme known as the Backward Induction Profits Sharing (BIPS) mechanism. The BIPS mechanism distributes profits fairly by taking into account the reduced network quality costs resulting from peak hour price negotiations between the ISPs and content providers. A detailed analysis of the BIPS mechanism reveals that it residency over other existing methods, including the Weighted Backward Induction Profits (WIPS) mechanism, in terms of ensuring the profitability of both ISPs and content providers. Furthermore, the BIPS mechanism outperforms the WIPS mechanism in reducing the risk of contract termination, particularly when content providers initiate such actions.

The standard approach to quantum mechanics relies on preparation of quantum states, followed by measurement of corresponding properties. In contrast, the preparation independence approach prioritizes measurement properties, defining quantum systems in terms of abstract states and concretized systems represented by Hilbert spaces and maps. Both frameworks are equivalent but distinct. This analysis reveals that any argument supporting one framework is automatically valid for the other.

In the landscape of cosmological models, $\alpha$-attractor models have emerged as strong contenders to describe the post-inflationary universe. This class of models has its own distinct characteristics, such as exponential potential curves, which are intertwined with the concept of $\alpha$-attractors. The mechanism of $\alpha$-attractors emerges when a particular field, exhibiting a constant rate of self-interaction, is embedded within a higher-dimensional multifield space. This unique property enables the $\alpha$-attractor model to be robust against the disturbances introduced by other fields in the space. The model's various parameters, namely $\alpha$ and $A$, play a significant role in predicting the universe's post-inflationary behavior, which in turn is influenced by the model's specific architecture. By exploring different model parameter combinations, we can gain valuable insights into the universe's history, thereby providing a direct link between the model's design and its predicted cosmological outcomes. The aim of this review is to offer a comprehensive overview of the $\alpha$-attractor model's theoretical framework, its predicted outcomes, and to provide a comparison with other well-established models, such as the $m^2$ and $P^2$ models. We have also highlighted some critical aspects that require further investigation in order to further develop and refine the $\alpha$-attractor model.

In the context of a quasi-Fuchsian hyperbolic three-dimensional manifold with a boundary that approaches infinity, its foliations measured at infinity closely resemble the extensions of the standard foliations measured at infinity for Fuchsian manifolds. The key difference lies in that these measured foliations can be made to closely resemble each other under certain conditions, specifically when the associated matrices representing the foliations' tangents can be made arbitrarily similar, regardless of the angles at which they approach the manifold's boundary. The goals of this research are first to demonstrate that when a non-peripheral lattice is used, the tangents of measured foliations at infinity can be made arbitrarily similar to the tangents of measured foliations at infinity for nearby Fuchsian manifolds. The second goal is to prove that when a non-peripheral lattice is used, the angles at which the foliations approach the manifold's boundary can be made arbitrarily similar to the angles at which the foliations approach the boundary of nearby Fuchsian manifolds. The proof of this involves showing the convergence of the foliations' development maps, which is in turn based on analyzing how the foliations' angles change as they approach the boundary of the manifold.

This study introduces novel mathematical tools for analyzing and forecasting portfolio performance across various time horizons. It utilizes a dynamic portfolio model that leverages real-time market data to estimate portfolio results over specified periods. By incorporating multiple asset configurations, the model enables the calculation of potential losses and gains for each portfolio strategy across different timelines. To facilitate forecasting, the paper adapts these formulas to a framework based on ARMA models, allowing the evaluation of future portfolio performance based on past results. Ultimately, the study demonstrates the model's practical uses in evaluating different asset investment strategies.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation recordings is hampered by poor quality due to background noise and the interpreter's experience.  To address this challenge, a method is developed to classify cardiac auscultation recordings into three conditions - normal, abnormal, and likely abnormal - by designing a classifier that can handle various levels of background noise and the mechanical distortion that occurs during digital heart sound recordings.  To test this method, twelve spiral tapetoires were used to record signal variations of four spiral tapetoires with a microphone.  Additionally, forty RSRp recordings with five types of background noise were created.  It is shown that the proposed method successfully differentiates between cardiac auscultation recordings with and without noise, and accurately classifies cardiac auscultation recordings with noise and distortion.  Importantly, the proposed method is the first to combine noise and distortion robustness for automatic heart sound classification.

In a 2021 study, we had developed a more accurate calculation for a specific nuclear transition in $^{133}$Cs using relativistic coupled-cluster theory. Recently, Roberts and Ginges raised concerns about our work, stating that our calculation contradicts existing nonrelativistic predictions made by other researchers and a small correction made by us. They suggested three possible explanations for this discrepancy. However, the actual cause lies in a mistake made in a previous calculation as pointed out by Pachucki in 2004, where the nonrelativistic correction was incorrectly assessed.

This study classifies all twists on a torus that exhibit symmetry corresponding to 2-dimensional crystallographic point groups. A twist on a torus can be viewed as a homeomorphism that preserves the torus's structure, and the twists characterized here are those that conform to the principles of the aforementioned point groups. The classification outcomes will be presented in a diagram, illustrating the relationships between various twists on a torus, and specifying the underlying topological invariants for each case.

This study examines how climate change is addressed in science fair projects submitted by US K-12 students. The projects are analyzed based on their themes, which reveal a lack of alignment between scientific research and the concerns of young people. Their projects exhibit a high level of cooperation and a strong desire for community involvement, yet their environmental focus is limited to individual issues rather than considering the broader social climate needed to address the climate crisis effectively. The research suggests that education focused on both scientific and social aspects of climate change could effectively engage the next generation in addressing this critical issue.

This study investigates multidimensional multidifferential operators acting on the space of multivariate polynomial functions within the context of the discrete Hardy space $H^1(\mathbb{Z}^d)$. To generalise existing operator theories, we introduce a novel approach based on the concept of fractional derivatives of step functions from $H^1(\mathbb{Z}^d)$. To achieve this, we utilise the discrete maximal operator and an invariant mean over $\mathbb{Z}^d$. By exploring some key properties of these operators, we establish essential estimates for any non-negative $s$, and our findings extend existing results from $L^1$ to $H^1$ and encompass the cases of bounded and unbounded kernels. We further establish estimates for multidifferential operators with bounded and unbounded kernels, and our work has implications for the study of fractional multidifferential operators in $L^p(\mathbb{Z}^d)$ for $1 < p \leq 1 + \frac{1}{d}$.

This study offers the first empirical evaluation of trustworthiness in auctions. We define an honest auction as one that accurately discloses its true revenue-generating mechanism, whereas a deceptive auction conceals this information. We develop and test two trustworthiness metrics, one of which is based on the concept of "asymmetric robustness" - the difference between an honest auction's and a deceptive auction's highest bidder values. We conducted multiple rounds of experiments involving auctions with unknown mechanisms, revealing that human bidders are unable to distinguish honest from deceptive auctions based on revenue patterns. As a result, bidder behavior in these auctions aligns with a theory predicting risk-dominated strategies, leading to revenue shortfalls for sellers in these situations. Conversely, in auctions with transparent mechanisms, bidder behavior matches predictions from a second-price auction model. Our findings suggest that trustworthiness has a tangible impact on auction performance, and that bidder incentives are strongly linked to the honesty of the auction process.

The explanation of accelerated cosmology is partially satisfactory but challenges to understanding the universe's early development persist. Our research focuses on the potential of a new symmetric teleparallel theory of gravity, denoted as $f(Q)$, where the non-metricity scalar $Q$ helps to address theoretical limitations imposed by metric-affine geometry. Our study examines how this theory restricts the emergence of isotropy in dynamically spatially homogeneous universes. Specifically, we investigate the isotropic universe models with one dimension invariant under rotation in order to analyze the theory's implications for the universe's early development. Our findings indicate that this theory prevents the universe from entering the isotropic stage unless the universe is already isotropic. Furthermore, when the theory is consistent with the universe's early development, it implies that the universe must have passed through a stage where it is expanding and anisotropic.

We establish a local parameterization for the Hessenberg variety $H(\blambda, \bu)$ associated with a given permutation $\blambda$ of type $A$. This involves developing a geometric vertex decomposition method and utilizing Grobner bases to encode Hessenberg functions to the multiplicity framework. By applying the vertex decomposition, we are able to reframe a specific set of Hessenberg varieties, denoted $H_{fr}(\blambda, \bu)$, as Fulton-Zelevinsky tilings of signed Young diagrams. This provides a connection between regular nilpotent Hessenberg varieties and Frobenius partitions. Furthermore, our analysis of $H_{fr}(\blambda, \bu)$ allows us to identify a specific subset, $H_{fr}^{s}(\blambda, \bu)$, characterized by "strictly skew-shaped" tilings, where we demonstrate that the variety is complete op-positiive.

Neural Painters leverage AI-powered models to create art, often utilizing GANs and style transfer technologies. Despite their potential, these painters struggle to deliver consistent high-quality output. To address this challenge, we introduce a new painting technique, gifting each neural brush a set of characteristics, thereby making it possible to paint with a wider range of strokes. We implement this approach by employing a generative brush model that can generate brushes with distinct textures, shapes, and sizes. To facilitate more controlled painting, we utilize a stroke generator model, allowing neural painters to execute pre-defined strokes instead of relying on the painter's internal stroke model. We evaluate the efficacy of this method in producing higher-quality paintings compared to existing neural painting methods.

We offer an innovative explanation for observed anomalies in $K$ and $B$ meson decay processes that involves the simultaneous resolution of two long-standing problems: the noted discrepancies in $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ and $R_K$ measurements. Within our model, the conflict can be resolved due to the presence of contributions from neutral currents, specifically the box diagram and $\epsilon_K$ contributions arising from the right-handed currents, interacting with flavor-singlet fields. Given that the flavor non-conserving operators in our model are heavily suppressed at quark level, we are able to circumvent the requirement for significant $\Delta S=1$ contribution, thereby avoiding the need for a further fine-tuning beyond natural expectations. Additionally, we have verified that our proposed solution adheres to the constraints of the Standard Model, specifically with regards to $\epsilon'/\epsilon$ and $R_K$ results, as well as obligations stemming from flavor and electroweak precision tests, while also verifying that LHC constraints are respected.

When conducting literature reviews, researchers often require assistance in comprehending difficult concepts, identifying connections between related studies, or pinpointing pivotal articles. However, current systems fall short in addressing researchers' queries due to the intricate nature of these questions, which often involve assumptions made in the research, differences in expertise, or knowledge deficits. A critical obstacle lies in the scarcity of comprehensive, annotated datasets that cater to the diverse needs of researchers. To bridge this gap, we have introduced QASPER, a groundbreaking dataset consisting of 794 questions posed by subject matter experts regarding 236 scientific papers in information systems. Each question on this dataset amounts to an inquiry based on multiple research papers, necessitating an answer that includes both the relevant citation information and a detailed explanation. The questions in this dataset were collectively addressed by four experienced professionals. The comprehensive Raw Data consists of 794 questions posed by subject matter experts regarding 236 scientific papers in information systems. Each question on this dataset amounts to an inquiry based on multiple research papers, necessitating an answer that includes both the relevant citation information and a detailed explanation. The questions in this dataset were collectively addressed by four experienced professionals.

In order to understand fast neutrino flavor instability in supernova events, two advanced simulations were conducted, one involving a massive 9 solar mass star explosion and the other, a 20 solar mass non-explosion. These studies revealed neutrino instabilities primarily occur within regions where neutrinos separate and near the shockwave barrier. In both scenarios, instabilities emerged due to electron neutrinos passing through the neutrino sphere and an area just inside it. This area experiences intense cooling and increased advection, causing neutrino frequencies to drop below a critical threshold, triggering instability. Within the shockwave barrier, instabilities were triggered by gradients in electron neutrino density and pressure. In both models, instabilities remained confined to small areas and had minimal impact on flavor mixing. Neutrino instability had no noticeable effect on either explosion or non-explosion events. These findings suggest model-specific variations don't significantly impact neutrino flavor instability properties.

Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) is characterized by short attention span and high levels of restlessness and impulsivity. The disorder's symptoms have significant personal and social consequences for individuals who suffer from it. Until now, diagnosing ADHD has relied on a combination of clinical evaluations and neuropsychological tests. Although these methods are effective, they are unable to provide insights into the disorder's underlying brain functions. Advances in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) technology allow researchers to study the brain's structure and function in detail, even in children. By analyzing data from functional MRI (fMRI) scans, researchers have been able to identify specific patterns in brain function that are associated with ADHD. One such network, responsible for attention control, has been found to be impaired in individuals with ADHD. To improve the accuracy of ADHD diagnosis, researchers have developed and trained deep learning models using comprehensive MRI data covering the entire brain. This study investigates whether excluding certain brain areas from the data affects the performance of deep learning models. By focusing on regions of the brain that are essential for attention control, researchers have found that certain areas, such as the cerebellum, are not crucial for this function. This discovery is consistent with existing knowledge about the cerebellum's role in attention deficit disorders. To determine which brain regions are essential for attention control, researchers employed an information-theoretic approach, which identified specific areas of the brain associated with ADHD. In a discrete-time sequence, the SISI model is used to simulate an outbreak, 
where the model's dynamics are determined by the product of two binary matrices, 
resulting in which-ever category the infected individuals move to, 
depending on whether they transmit the infection to others or not. 
We develop a parameterized model, to be reported on, by introducing probability values for transitions. 
Based on this parameterized model, we develop a nonlinear system of equations, 
from which we derive an eight-dimensional system of equations for the overall outbreak cases, 
ultimately leading to an eight-dimensional system of equations for the overall outbreak cases, 
along with the conditions of asymptotic stability for the equilibrium points and the relevant numerical examples.

This demonstration showcases the MadDog system, a comprehensive web-based platform developed for identifying and resolving acronyms within general texts and datasets. MadDog is comprised of two primary components: a machine learning-based algorithm and a knowledge database featuring extensively annotated examples. We will highlight how users can leverage MadDog for both dataset annotation and general texts, as well as introduce the system's capabilities, which include batch processing for large datasets and on-the-fly processing for individual texts. Additionally, we will illustrate the system's functionality in addressing the dataset annotation challenge in the SemEval 2021 tasks 6 and 7.

Quantum Hall junctions that control electronic flow using electromagnetic interference have the potential to be used in quantum information systems and microelectromechanical devices. Despite their promising use, the interference's impact on the thermoelectric properties of these junctions remains poorly understood. Investigating quantum Hall junctions consisting of various paths and electron phases, we discovered that electromagnetic interference can switch on and off the thermoelectric effect and generate heat differences across the junctions. Our findings reveal that heat currents can be fully blocked or allowed to pass through by adjusting interference patterns, leading to enhanced heat rectification. We have provided theoretical explanations for the observed phenomena and analyzed the potential for efficient heat rectification.

Our proposed DNA-storage system presents a novel architecture that leverages the properties of hierarchical data structures to efficiently manage DNA data updates across various levels of the data structure's tree structure. By introducing 'don't-care' nucleotide bases in the read-out process, our approach achieves highly customizable, flexible data retrieval with exceptionally high data update rates through simultaneous sequencing of overlapping reads. These capabilities enable us to significantly enhance the DNA storage update speed, reaching up to three orders of magnitude improvement in optimal scenarios, aided by an intelligent placement strategy that facilitates efficient data updates at all levels of the tree structure.

Topological insulators represent a significant phenomenon in modern condensed matter research, characterized by exceptional properties of exotic matter states that facilitate unidirectional and unobstructed electron flow and enable precise measurements of the Hall conductivity. Current research focuses on various forms of topological insulators, including those based on Z, Zn, Zy, and other higher-dimensional polyhedra known for their unique properties. Recent breakthroughs have led to the creation of topological insulators using sound waves, light waves, and caustic patterns, providing a wealth of opportunities for theoretical analysis and experimental exploration. A 2022 study provides an updated overview of recent developments in the field and offers fresh perspectives on the subject.

In oscillatory media, regions with increased excitation frequency serve as pacemakers, producing waves at their local frequency when coupled to responding elements. To generate insight into the mechanisms behind speed adjustments, we developed an analytical model, generalizing the results of Kuznetsov et al. (2003) and applying them to various systems. The model considers both relaxing and excitatory responses to better match the behavior of specific systems, as illustrated in the case studies involving cardiac cells.

A fundamental concept in quantum theory, the total entropy of a quantum state measures its disorder or uncertainty. Measuring entropy using traditional methods often necessitates expensive computations. We present two innovative, resource-constrained approaches, one classical and one quantum, that allow for approximating entropy up to a specified margin without proportional scaling. We examine both approaches in detail, starting with a novel classical algorithm based on a well-known metric and an averaging procedure. We then develop a quantum approach leveraging rapid measurement techniques and entropy estimation methods. Our findings indicate the quantum method outperforms the classical method in terms of efficiency, achieving better approximation ratios with significantly less resource usage. We further compare the quantum method to another, highly efficient quantum method, finding it has advantages in terms of scalability and practical application with real-world data.

As AI systems grow in size and diversity, understanding their underlying technical foundations becomes increasingly important for analyzing broader ecosystem trends and implications. AI systems are comprised of multiple technical elements: data repositories, computation platforms, and implementation frameworks, which collectively define what an AI system is and enable its development and operation. To investigate these essential technical components, we established a comprehensive database called AI Technical Factors, which tracks various data storage, computation, and implementation methods across multiple organizations. Initially covering seven major companies, this database has the potential to be expanded to study the broader AI landscape. By examining existing data, we obtained key insights into storage and computation practices among leading AI players, including average storage capacities, computation durations, and the prevalence of distributed computation systems. Our analysis also shed light on usage patterns of cloud services, such as compute and storage utilization, and revealed differences in these patterns among distinct computation methods and organizations. Furthermore, we obtained quantitative information on the structure of AI systems, including pipeline lengths and components, which provided insights into the diversity of systems and their potential for future growth. By delving into these detailed technical metrics, we can gain a more nuanced understanding of the AI ecosystem and explore various research questions, such as how different computation methods affect data storage and pipeline distribution, the prevalence of duplicate pipelines across distinct organizations, and the system complexity of various AI systems and potential drivers.

Electrocardiograms are widely used to identify individuals' heart conditions through a process called ICD coding. The ICD coding system helps healthcare professionals identify existing or potential conditions revealed by ECGs. The classification process for ICD codes is usually done manually, requiring a lot of time and effort. We've proposed an semi-self-supervised multilabel classification method by integrating codification to facilitate automated ICD coding. We used pre-trained cardiovascular models to fine-tune our approach, which we demonstrated on a large dataset. The results show that our method significantly improves accuracy and reduces computational costs compared to traditional supervised learning techniques.

Let $R$ be a polynomial ring in $n$ variables over a field $k$. A monomial ideal $I$ within this ring is considered. This paper explores nearly Cohen-Macaulay simplicial complexes and provides specific classifications for certain types of ideals, including polymatroidal Veronese type and transversal polymatroidal ideals, along with illustrative examples.

Achieving significant breakthroughs on practical quantum computers likely requires untested assumptions from human learning, such as not differentiating between data categories or using labeled data. Unsupervised learning may offer a more natural model of machine learning, while guided learning could provide a pathway to overcome current performance limitations on quantum machines. We conducted a study to explore these concepts on superconducting quantum devices using various circuits and techniques. Our research showed that quantum circuits with fewer qubits can facilitate insight into complex systems, but face challenges in replicating traditional machine learning algorithms due to differences in computational architecture. Despite these discrepancies, quantum machines can still make informed decisions in complex systems, and our study provides a foundation for further research into quantum-guided learning algorithms.

Our team has conducted a comprehensive search through the KMTNet data and has identified 25 new planetary-mass candidates from the 2018 prime-field observations. Out of these candidates, 11 were found to be relocatable, and upon further analysis,  four were deemed to be temporary eclipse objects, and one was classified as an artifact. Ultimately, we obtained two new planetary mass anomalies, each consisting of multiple data points, and dubbed them MOA-2018-BAN_603 and MOA-2018-BLE-193. By applying parallax measurements from the Gaia dataset, we calculated the likelihoods of these two objects being planets, and as a result, both were deemed probable planetary mass objects. MOA-2018-BAN_603 was determined to have a mass of approximately 9.52 Earth masses and an estimated radius of 2.75 times that of Earth, while MOA-2018-BLE-193 was found to have a mass of around 4.20 Earth masses and a radius equivalent to 1.13 times that of Earth. Our analysis added to the existing list of small-bodied stars with planetary mass objects, and the data has been made accessible through the KMTNet Anomaly Browser for further examination.

Differentiable rendering has gained significant attention in the computer vision community, with applications like inverse rendering and simulation. This research expands the scope of differentiable rendering to encompass non-trivial scenes that incorporate accurate shadow computation. We introduce a novel, efficient algorithm for differentiating through ray-tracing using sphere-based casting, effectively enabling the use of gradient-based optimization methods for various inverse problems. To accommodate general shapes, we employ a unified volumetric model that accommodates arbitrary materials, allowing it to model both thin objects and high-resolution textures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through successful demonstrations of two inverse problems: recovering object positions from a scene snapshot, and generating realistic textures from real-world scenes using optimization techniques.

Recent research on transportation networks leverages large datasets, enabling the acquisition of big data in transport fields. This growing information enables the enhancement of conventional conventional transportation models, which traditionally relied on classic statistical theory. This paper focuses on a general framework for a conventional transportation model based on a nonparametric approach that incorporates Bayesian statistics. The proposed framework involves estimating an origin-destination demand matrix by converting an observed link performance matrix through a specified structure. In this way, a conventional transportation model can be developed without presuming a specific probability distribution, which is often not justifiable without robust theoretical support. The model's reliability is evaluated using modules such as the mean squared error, mean absolute error, mean absolute error percentage, mean squared error percentage, chi-squared statistic, Cramér-V statistic, Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic, and Kullback-Leibler distance. The results show that the mean squared error, mean absolute error, mean absolute error percentage, and mean squared error percentage are reliable measures of fit for continuous variables but are not sufficient to assess fit for categorical variables, necessitating the use of the Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic or Kullback-Leiber distance. The chi-squared statistic is effective for categorical variables but gives preference to underdispersion, highlighting a significant limitation. The reliability of the origin-destination demand matrix is evaluated using modules such as the mean squared error, mean absolute error, mean absolute error percentage, mean squared error percentage, chi-s

In an array of nonlinear oscillators with randomly taken frequencies and strengths, we discovered three distinct phases in which the phases of the oscillators become synchronized.  Specifically, when the overall strength of connections within the array is weak, a narrow frequency range leads to a sharp peak in synchronization of the oscillators' phases, while two other phases of synchronization show no notable frequency dependencies.  We found that when the overall strength of connections within the array is strong, a wide frequency range leads to a significant decrease in synchronization of the oscillators' phases, and also observed that at intermediate connection strengths, a wide frequency range leads to a significant decrease in synchronization of the oscillators' phases.  Additionally, we analyzed the condition for the widest range of frequencies for different types of oscillator arrangements and network patterns.

The well-documented Aldous-Broder and Wilson algorithms create random spanning trees through random walks, and this research highlights their equivalence using a temporary 'collapse' operation. By applying this operation, Wilson's algorithm's 'tree-rejection' component can be transformed into a 'edge-rejection' process identical to that in Broder's algorithm. Furthermore, this research proposes a two-stage framework for generating uniform spanning trees, incorporating the temporary 'collapse' operation, offering an alternative to both Wilson's and Broder's algorithms.

This work presents a comprehensive music dataset named MusicTM-Dataset that enhances cross-modal retrieval capabilities by offering a diverse collection of:

- Musical scores, encompassing simplified and complex notation
- Song lyrics, covering short poems and extended verses
- Musical audio

Our dataset comprises 42,622 musical scores and 16,039 lyrics, meticulously annotated alongside 13,778 corresponding audio tracks. The dataset's development from scratch necessitates innovative approaches for data gathering, processing, and annotation, posing challenging problems to be addressed. 

To validate our method, several rigorous experiments are conducted, utilizing state-of-the-art techniques to establish baseline cross-modal retrieval performance on the MusicTM-Dataset. Notably, our research demonstrates significant advancements in retrieving musical scores through audio and lyrics, achieving exceptional results particularly for score-audio retrieval.

The MusicTM-Dataset, along with its accompanying code, are publicly available for download at: https://github.com/dxd6680/MusicTM-Dataset.

One major obstacle when utilizing Linked Data lies in developing intuitive and user-friendly interfaces accessible to individuals who aren't technologically inclined. To address this, Ontodia enables diagrammatic data visualization, illustrated in this study with the Wikidata dataset. We've introduced enhancements to a natural language interface that facilitates the exploration and querying of Linked Data entities. By utilizing distributional semantic models to identify and rank entity properties associated with user input in Ontodia, the method demonstrates improved results in enhancing user experience during visual data exploration.

In the nonlinear Schrödinger equation with variable dispersion, our computational findings indicate that dark solitons maintain stability under defocusing conditions, regardless of increased dispersion. However, under focusing conditions, there is a threshold value for enhanced dispersion beyond which the dark solitons become destabilized and start oscillating in the vicinity of their initial positions, leading to the formation of small-brightness solitary waves and increased transmission of radiation in the direction of propagation. We have developed a theoretical explanation for these behaviors using the nonlinear Schrödinger equation's numerical mode amplitude equations, which indicate that dark solitons can remain stable under focusing conditions if the linear and higher-order dispersion coefficients have opposite signs but are proportional to each other in magnitude.

When developers incorporate guidance mechanisms into their applications, a common aim is to minimize cognitive load and enhance users' performance. However, numerous guidance structures already exist, each with its own strengths and weaknesses, often uncritically emulated in new systems. This paper introduces the LOTSE structure, a guidance method that leverages expertise to control the flow of information, ensuring it remains relevant and timely. We draw inspiration from existing approaches, addressing their inherent flaws, and employ a cognitive architecture grounded in human capabilities. In contrast to conventional guidance structures, LOTSE is exceptionally adaptable, empowering developers to incorporate various expertise sources and seamlessly integrate guidance and feedback mechanisms. Our evaluation involves a benchmark task, conducted by professional developers and undergraduate students, who compared LOTSE to three established guidance structures, revealing better performance and increased satisfaction rates for LOTSE users.

Low aspect ratio stellarators have a demonstrated potential for excellent magnetic confinement and have garnered interest for integrated magnetic research. We have developed an approach to enhance coil design in low-aspect-ratio stellarators capable of producing both axisymmetric and non-axisymmetric fields. This modified coil design, based on quasi-classical optimization, significantly improves their performance by maximizing their magnetic energy density, an important metric for effective plasma confinement. We have successfully integrated the proposed coil design with the NCSX stellarator, which is capable of producing both axisymmetric and null field configurations. The enhanced coil design offers considerable advantages, boasting a 30% increase in magnetic energy density and a 25% reduction in coil volume required to produce a null field, while also maintaining excellent planar and quasi-planar accessibility in outer regions. This improved design exhibits more efficiently varying orthogonal fields and can accommodate essential singularities within the null field region without compromising its quality. We have explored two possible scenarios for integrating the quasi-null stellarator configurations into the NCSX design, both of which preserve the original D-shaped axisymmetric core and utilize the outer regions to generate the required null fields. The first scenario, based on quasi-null coils, demonstrates a 23% reduction in magnetic energy density, while the second scenario, featuring quasi-modulated coils, exhibits a 24% reduction in magnetic energy density. The employed methodology to generate the quasi-modulated coils is general and can be extended to other integrated scenarios and configurations.

Achieving uniform temperature distribution within gas-solid fixed beds is critical for optimizing catalytic reactions and safety in industrial processes.  However, temperature disparities often result in hot spots that could lead to safety hazards, unscheduled equipment degradation, and uneven catalyst activity.  Studying temperature variations in gas-solid fixed beds has been difficult, mainly because of the limitations imposed by measuring techniques and the beds' reactive and combustible nature.  To overcome this challenge, researchers used rapid MRI to directly measure temperature distributions within fixed beds made of nickel oxide and gas flows of air and nitrogen.  The results revealed temperature differences of up to 100 K, primarily based on gas flow rates and not bulk densities, as observed in the beds' various states.  The findings provided valuable insights into temperature arrangements, which could inform future applications, including catalyst activation, process control, and reactor design and operation.

Within systems composed of multiple species, each represented by distinct colors or symbols, we investigate the spontaneous assembly of clusters consisting of shared building blocks, applying both a theoretical approach and numerical simulations. We leverage a theoretical framework known as the Boltzmann-Gibbs entropy formula to derive aggregate formation probabilities, which are subsequently validated through simulations employing a lattice-based model. By analyzing both the theoretical and simulated results, we obtain precise definitions for three distinct types of cluster formation. Moreover, we observe a symmetry in the outcomes, resulting from the arbitrary assignment of species and colors, which yields two sets of formation probabilities. Ultimately, we demonstrate that our findings can effectively predict aggregate structures, even those not initially considered.

Using the Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager on the Solar Dynamics Observatory, we studied how a major solar flare event affected a large active region (AR) on the sun. The observation revealed how a major solar flare drew energy from smaller areas within the active region and how it caused these areas to move rapidly. The calculation showed that the regions experienced a significant loss of magnetic field strength, and analyzed data indicated that the regions rotated quickly in response to the flare, with some areas reaching rotation speeds of up to 6.8 degrees per hour. The findings suggest that the regions underwent significant disturbance in their magnetic fields, and suggested that this disturbance could be associated with the flare. The movement of the regions matched the expected rotation speed associated with magnetic field changes, and the results indicated that the regions experienced a significant decrease in their magnetic field strength, and the areas rotated quickly in response to the flare, with the speed of rotation increasing as the distance decreased, and the results matched the expected rotation speed associated with magnetic field changes, and the results indicated that the regions experienced a significant disturbance in their magnetic field due to the flare.

Mather's b-principle is a highly effective theory for addressing extension and categorification challenges, and it has had a significant influence on modern mathematics since its first public presentation in 2018. The soundness of the b-principle relies on three fundamental components: the M-theory, the Nuklakov theorem, and the Fragile b-principle. While the M-theory and Nuklavarov theorems originate from Mather's work, the Fragile b-principle was introduced by I. Zhukovskiy. 

The b-principle's applicability to numerous recent breakthroughs, such as the solution to the Lagrangian Floer practice, the Andrei Okounkov's challenge, and the Gromov incompatibility problem, not to mention the proof of the fundamental equivalence hypothesis, demonstrates its immense value. The b-principle's impact is also evident in fields like Mirror symmetry, where it facilitated the creation of an extensive list of test cases, and led to the development of new techniques still in the process of being introduced.

The b-principle has also been successfully applied to combinatorial mathematics, resulting in a plethora of new theorems and classifications, and its influence can be seen in the fields of Topological mechanics, Homotopy theory, and Algebraic combinatorics. The b-principle's applications extend beyond the fields mentioned above, and it is evident that its influence will continue to grow in the future.

This study compares the efficiency of Balancing Domain Decomposition by Constraints (BDDC) and Algebraic Multigrid (AMG) methods for solving finite element models in cardiac mechanics on various machine architectures. The impact of different saddle point solvers and grid refinement strategies on the performance and scalability of these methods is also examined. The analysis is conducted across different architectures, ranging from local high-performance computers to a national supercomputing cluster and a cloud infrastructure. The research sheds light on the pros and cons of BDDC and AMG solutions in terms of scalability, flexibility, ease of use, and ease of implementation, thereby informing practitioners in cardiac mechanics with essential insights to enhance the scalability of their computations.

The ever-growing influence of User-Generated Content (UGC) underscores the need to gain insight into user behavior and content creation practices. Social tagging systems are particularly adept at gathering detailed information about user interactions, making them ideal for studying UGC habits. By examining data from multiple tagging systems, we investigate users' content creation approaches, including the patterns of resource creation and delegation, user collaboration, and content sharing over time. Our analysis reveals users to be sophisticated content creators, employing established strategies such as expert delegation, and developing intricate temporal patterns, like production bursts and fluctuations. Interestingly, our results show that users' behavior converges towards consistent patterns as they progress in the system.

Recently, controllable acoustic shielding and redirection in water have been achieved at frequencies below 1 MHz using microacoustic metagratings, constructed using two-photon photolithography in a rigid, porous material. This paper presents an innovative development of this technique at much higher frequencies, approximately 10 MHz. A novel, transparent, and lightweight microacoustic metagrating, comprised of a hexagonal arrangement of fine tubes, has been manufactured using the 3D printing technique called stereolithography, utilizing photopolymer materials with acoustic properties similar to those used in the previous study. Using theoretical models and experimental proof-of-pilot tests, the proposed metagrating has been shown to effectively redirect sound waves at a 90-degree angle, offering insights into its underlying acoustic resonance principles. This breakthrough has the potential to advance acoustic wave control and manipulation in multiple fields, including bioacoustics and acoustic energy harvesting.

This paper primarily focuses on the long-term behavior of strong solutions to the two-dimensional compressible FENE ribbon model. Utilizing the Fourier splitting technique, we demonstrate the optimal time decay rate of the solutions, $\ln^{-l}(e+t)$, for any positive integer $l$. Additionally, we have found that the time decay rate is optimal as $t$ tends to infinity.

Implementing Internet Architecture over Bitcoin (IAB) facilitates mobile payments on the internet, allowing users to access public services while maintaining control of their bitcoin.  The IAB protocol, implemented on the bitcoin network, was initially shown to be insecure, particularly vulnerable to attacks like the double-spending problem.  A secure IAB implementation requires addressing this issue, which is the primary focus of this paper.  By examining attacks on IAB, this work proposes a flexible and efficient solution to ensure secure mobile payments, including new bitcoin transactions types, updated IAB protocol specifications, and a mobile payment system architecture.  The paper also explores the challenges and potential applications of IAB in the future.

In this study, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of three global sensitivity analysis methods on five leading ordering methods to determine their suitability in assessing hyperparameter sensitivity for computational evolutionary models. Our investigation focuses on the Kovalevsky model, a mathematical model that is not applicable in real-world scenarios, but is used to test the effectiveness of ranking methods. The study compares the efficiency of three methods – Sobol, Saltelli, and Monte Carlo – in mirroring the behavior of an underlying goodness-of-fit metric called the lack of fit. The assessment of these methods is based on three indicators: replication diversity, ranking consistency, and predictive accuracy. The results show that Sobol methods outperform others in analyzing sensitivity, while Monte Carlo methods excel in predictive tasks. Additionally, we find that no method is superior to others in examining diversity and ranking consistency, suggesting that different methods may be applicable in different evaluation contexts.

The paper presents a series of reasoning and mathematical proofs supported by both theoretical and experimental evidence suggesting that in quantum theory, the wave function's magnitude squared should be directly proportional to the likelihood density at any given point in a measurement. These arguments draw upon analogies with classical mechanics, statistical physics, and the Born interpretation, as well as recent findings from quantum mechanics and electrodynamics that follow the wave theory.

Despite notable breakthroughs in reinforcement learning, numerous significant hurdles remain when applying it to dynamic and ever-changing problems common in critical domains, including robotics and complex gameplay. Reinforcement learning models generally struggle to generalize effectively when confronted with new tasks beyond their training data. In order to address this issue and evaluate the capabilities of future models, we create L2Explorer, a groundbreaking benchmark platform that challenges lifelong reinforcement learning through an endless stream of open-ended tasks. This innovative platform offers a vast range of adaptive strategies, allowing researchers and developers to experiment with different approaches and understand their generalizability and efficiency. We provide detailed analysis and comparison of 14 baseline methods, as well as an analysis of the results based on hyperparameter adjustments, which sheds light on the underlying dynamics of the L2Explorer environment. The study findings suggest that, although certain techniques have inherent potential in this environment, context-specific adjustments through experimentation are necessary to achieve success. We hope that L2Explorer will serve as a standard platform for evaluating the abilities of future models in this field.

Liger, a next-generation infrared device at the W. M. Keck Observatory, will be paired with the Keck All-sky Precision Adaptive-optics system to optimize performance. By covering the wavelength range from 0.81 micrometers to 2.45 micrometers, Liger combines multiple observing modes, offering various spatial scales and fields of view. To process data from Liger, a customized data processing system and software framework are being developed to accurately determine various performance metrics in real-time while maintaining a quick data transmission rate to the control system. The system will also enable users to visualize their data in real-time and execute on-board data reduction tasks.

This study uncovers a broad class of non-trivial, travelling waves arising alongside Couette flow in 2D Euler equation models. It demonstrates that these waves can develop finite-amplitude distortions at any rate, given sufficient Reynolds number. Furthermore, numerical simulations reveal the presence of a critical threshold above which these waves start to emerge. The research also establishes a hypothesis linking these travelling waves to a new type of instability, one that's inherently three-dimensional in nature.

We experimentally control the linear polarization of exciton-polariton condensates using optical pulses, achieving either uniform polarization or bimodal coupling to left- and right-circularized modes.  By combining cut-off frequency tuning and refractive index modulation in a microcavity, we demonstrate complete polarization switching, decoupling, and re-coupling of polarization-distinguishable modes.  Analyzing system response, we find that bimodal coupling functionality survives despite losses, with a system anisotropy insensitivity to cavity loss parameters.  Optimization of pulse energy also allows us to overcome thermal effects and gain control over the system's response, facilitating reliable all-optical manipulation of exciton-polariton condensates in microcavities.

The COVID-19 pandemic has caused global devastation, with South Africa being an exception due to limited access to reliable COVID-19 data. To address this issue, our research used open-source and publicly available data to develop a COVID-19 visualization platform, which enabled decision-makers to monitor the outbreak's progression. By combining multiple data sources, we overcame the problem of limited COVID-19 data in South Africa, making it possible to compare the country's trends with international developments. Furthermore, our platform allowed policymakers to explore various 'what-if' scenarios by adjusting demographic variables and evaluating the impact on reported cases. By leveraging data analytics and machine learning, we identified key insights that could inform policy decisions, such as targeting provinces with the highest case numbers and focusing on population groups with the highest infection rates. Ultimately, our study demonstrated the importance of transparent data sharing and collaborative data-driven decision making, particularly during global health crises like the COVID-19 pandemic.

Freiman's 3k-4 theorem generally posits that if subsets A and B, which have a combined size of n, exhibit an average difference of at most d, then there exists a subset C of A intersecting B, with a size of at least n - 3n/4, implying an internal sum within the subset C that differs by at most 3d. In this revised form, we seek to broaden the scope, allowing for the possibility of an internal sum not attained by C when d is a multiple of 1/n for a set containing n elements.

In medical contexts, diverse data forms typically coexist, but projects tend to concentrate on a single data type, overlooking the potential benefits of combining modes. This proposal seeks to address this shortcoming by introducing a novel approach that integrates various data modes and proposes a comprehensive solution for combined feature extraction, dimension reduction, and classification tasks. To validate its effectiveness, we conducted extensive experiments on public datasets for diabetic macular disorders and glaucoma, while another submission built upon a similar idea, though slightly differently implemented, yielded comparable results and interesting variations in performance.

The COVID-19 pandemic has led to unprecendented economic and societal impacts globally. With no vaccine available at the start of the outbreak in Wuhan, China, the Chinese government implemented strict lockdown measures to contain the spread of the disease. To combat the crisis, hospitals in the region were overwhelmed, leading to a shortage of medical resources. To cope with the emergency situation, a specialized ICU was established for severe COVID-19 patients requiring immediate medical attention. To differentiate critically ill patients from less severe ones, healthcare professionals relied heavily on radiologists' interpretations of chest X-ray images, which provided vital insights into patients' respiratory conditions. Since chest X-ray images often revealed distinct patterns related to ICU admission symptoms such as fever and cough, researchers explored ways to identify specific patterns associated with these indicators. Specifically, this study aimed to identify unique features present in the ICU admission group's chest X-ray images compared to non-ICU admission patients.

This article delves into the theoretical and numerical aspects of recovering embedded spheres and their periodicities within an infinite medium via transmission eigenvalue problems. The extended perfect matched layer method is employed to formulate an integral equation for spherical boundaries, which in turn facilitates convergence of eigenfunctions as radius approaches infinity. Furthermore, we investigate Dirichlet-to-Neumann mappings and introduce a large-scale approximate problems involving an integral equation for each embedded sphere. Convergence of these approximate problems is demonstrated, and a continuously-improving sequence of piecewise constant functions is found to converge to the boundary shape of each sphere. These methods are validated by various numerical examples.

To expand a dialogue system's capabilities and facilitate its practical use, it is essential to identify novel user intentions that are not accounted for in its trained data. This paper proposes a novel intent discovery approach, which leverages a pre-trained language model to effectively explore unknown intentions in dialogue data. Specifically, our method employs contrastive learning to capture the intent structure within conversations, thereby enabling the discovery of new intents. Moreover, we introduce a intent segmentation task to segment multiple intents within a single utterance. Experimental results on two diverse datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our method in identifying novel user intentions.

The space of universal simplicial collections, denoted as $\mathcal{C}$mfsU, can be interpreted as a simplicial group when equipped with the glueing operation, which combines collection maps for common bases. This observation builds upon the notion of a group-like space framework and applies the theory of functors to map sub-bases within a fixed set, as defined in [1].

Consider any finite group $G$ and a prime number $p$. We want to count how many subgroups of $G$ have order divisible by the prime number $p$. Let's denote this number as $N_p(G)$. Research suggests that $N_2(G)$ has an upper limit of $2^{\frac{\log_2 |G|}{C} +1}$, where the constant $C$ is approximately 1.64406. We've discovered that the same inequality applies to $N_p(G)$ for any prime number $p$, with a different constant $C_p$. Furthermore, we've found that the logarithm base $p$ of $N_p(G)$ is bounded by a constant times $\frac{|G|}{p-1} + O(\log |G|)$. These results demonstrate the existence of an explicit upper limit on the number of subgroups of order $p$ in $G$, and the previous result on $N_2(G)$ is a specific instance of this finding.

This paper undertakes an in-depth examination of the ABS H2 equation, a member of the Adres-Besselhuber family, which exhibits unique properties when evaluated on certain lattice structures, enabling the identification of exact solutions via a straightforward lattice-based method.

This paper delves into visual relationship detection tasks, specifically focusing on removing incorrect relationships in annotated datasets. Current optimization techniques for VRD tasks are inefficient in eliminating erroneous positives, resulting from incorrectly predicted relationships between existing dataset entities. To address this issue, we introduce VRD-Negative Mining (VRNMin), a novel framework that aims to overcome the challenge. By incorporating a multi-stage verification process involving the augmentation of dataset samples, the enhancement of model accuracy, and the updating of annotation labels, the proposed framework significantly improves the accuracy of optimal solutions and the reliability of predicted relationships. Through comprehensive experiments on three diverse datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework and highlight its potential to be a long-term solution for VRD tasks. The implemented framework can be accessed at: https://github.com/MinGaoPy/VRD-NM.

We investigate the quantum correlation cost associated with weak measurements on a pair of qubits that are either perfectly aligned or perfectly anti-aligned. For all possible measurement strengths, our findings indicate that the correlation cost is zero for aligned qubits and finite for anti-aligned qubits. Furthermore, the cost is not only dependent on the measurement strength but also on the specific basis in which the measurements are performed. Notably, when performing measurements in the eigenbases of any single qubit, our results show that the correlation cost is quantifiable in terms of trace norms, resulting in a correlation cost of zero for aligned qubits and a correlation cost of $\log_2(\sqrt{\eta^2+\eta(1-\eta)})$ for anti-aligned qubits, for a given measurement strength $\eta$.

The rising tide of social media usage brings along a crushing subset of data, a significant portion of which is comprised of images and text. Current techniques for extracting social relationships from visual content rely on discrete models, with most using separate agents to process different media types. In contrast, an end-to-end network has been devised to derive a social relationship graph from multimedia data by employing a unified framework, one that leverages a common currency to guide an agent through the exploration of a mutual representation space. This novel approach is given expressional warmth via a neural network, comprised of multiple layers, with each layer serving as a node in the social relationship graph. Upon training this network, the social relationship graph is rendered differentiable, enabling backpropagation during the optimization process. Through extensive testing on existing benchmark data sets, the developed end-to-end network has exceeded previous results, solidifying a common currency's value in social relationship extraction and guiding future research in this area.

To address the issue of module interaction in vision recognition models, we introduce a multi-headed communication passing network called Dynamic Graph Communication Passing Network, which effectively facilitates communication between modules by adjusting the way information is shared and processed based on the characteristics of individual features. This approach is particularly useful for models with multiple modules and can be applied to various tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. We implement this idea in Vision Recognition models and achieve notable improvements in performance. For instance, the model achieves a remarkable 7.7% improvement in the top-1 accuracy for ImageNet with just 0.27M extra parameters when compared to a basic multi-head attention network. Furthermore, it delivers a 2.7% improvement in the mAP for COCO object detection with 0.07M fewer parameters when compared to Faster R-CNN with Multi-head Attention.

Optimized hardware is often required in embedded systems, leading to the need for efficient resource allocation through Multiple Constant Multiplication (MCM). One approach to solving MCM involves polynomial division based solutions. However, these consume additional hardware for the multiplier. To minimize hardware costs, we focus on MCM circuits using adders, proposing new models and algorithms that can handle any number of constants, scalars, and vectors, with support for shared multipliers. Compared to previous methods, our approach exhibits lower hardware costs, comprising fewer units and bits. To verify our model's validity and evaluate its efficiency, we conducted exhaustive searches within specified constraints. The results demonstrate our algorithm's ability to reduce hardware costs by 30% overall, with particular reductions of 29.2% for single constant MCM and 31.5% for vector MCM.

The intersection of quantum computing and deep neural networks has a promising future in addressing the limitations of current neural networks, such as their widespread use among data scientists despite lack of clear biological plausibility. Quantum deep learning has gained momentum in recent years, leading to increased research and development. This paper delves into the foundational aspects and clinical trials of quantum deep learning, covering essential concepts, pioneering approaches, and potential applications. It also explores challenging areas such as quantum hardware instability and the need for more comprehensive data sets.

The radio frequency (RF) accelerator community submitted its findings to the 2021 Snowmass proceedings, focusing on innovative R&D endeavors that have the potential to significantly transform the field of high-energy physics (HEP).  As the global supply chain struggles with constraints, there's a pressing need for breakthroughs in RF technology to ensure the implementation of future HEP projects as well as other critical applications.  This report outlines various areas of research and development, highlighting opportunities for collaboration between HEP and non-HEP sectors, and suggests a course of action for the AF7-rf topical group to effectively address emerging issues and drive progress in RF accelerators.

In the near future, physicists anticipate that the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) will discover new physics. However, the specific characteristics and energy thresholds of this new physics remain unknown. It's probable that insights gleaned from LHC data will require supplementary information obtained from a lepton collider to conduct a thorough investigation. This text discusses the underlying principles, accelerator layout, and detector development for a high-energy Muon Collider as well as the difficulties inherent in the machine and its detector environment.

Higher-frequency waves in relativistic hydrodynamics arise from fluid acceleration, 
causing deviations from the adiabatic sound wave profile, deviating from the 
standard $1/\omega$ dispersion relationship. We've re-examined the linearized 
wave equations for relativistic hydrodynamics, obtaining first-principles expressions 
for wave propagation in ideal and viscous fluids, with and without a chemical 
potential. Previous analyses on viscous fluids assumed the standard Einstein relation, 
resulting in a $1/\omega^2$ dispersion relationship; however, with Einstein relations 
violated, due to $\omega$ depending on both $k$ and $\omega$, a distinct 
long-wavelength behavior emerges, differing from both ideal and high-damping cases.

Primordial black holes are hypothesized as potential dark matter candidates and could be produced in large quantities through gravitational collapse of early universe matter and cosmic strings. In a study, it's demonstrated that ultralight bosons can be produced in high quantities via a process called Bose-Einstein condensation and subsequently fragment into black holes. Specifically, it's shown that as these black holes weigh less than the mass of radio particles, they naturally emit radio signals. As a result, it's estimated that if these black holes constitute all or a portion of dark matter, the diffuse radio background observed by LOFAR and PAPER experiments could be intensified by orders of magnitude due to the signal from these black holes. Moreover, it's found that the prediction of PBHs contributing to the dark matter, combined with the detection of the diffuse radio background, increases the likelihood of the hypothesis.

To achieve secure computation on untrusted architectures like PCs, Homomorphic Encryption enables computing on encrypted data, and the TFHE library is a leading implementation of this concept. However, its high overhead makes it impractical for general use cases, necessitating novel processor designs like the Virtual Safeguard Platform. This processor addresses the issue of supporting multi-bit gates within TFHE's circuit-based evaluation method. Our solution involves developing a Virtual Safeguard Unit and an HEU (Homomorphic Encryption Unit) to handle encrypted data and introducing a custom pipeline architecture with five stages to speed up evaluation processing. By overcoming the high overhead and limited gate depth limitations, our processor enables increased flexibility and a higher rate of processed bits per clock cycle. Results show that VSP can handle more computations per second than current processors using traditional methods.

We have developed a polynomial-time approximate solution algorithm with a guarantee of nearly flawless performance for general-valued optimization problems. This improvement builds upon prior methods, primarily designed for linear optimization problems, and is attributed to an innovative application of convex programming with constrained sparse data. This new method can be utilized to establish PTAS for numerous sparse regression problems.

Recent advancements in NLP have been propelled forward by pre-trained models such as RoBERTa and Elephants. These pre-trained models offer efficient solutions for classification, regression, and machine translation tasks, achieving results on par with state-of-the-art models. To further optimize task adaptation, we introduce novel techniques to streamline unsupervised and few-shot learning processes. Specifically, we utilize a weighted average to aggregate representations from multiple model layers, and demonstrate through experiments on BERT and Elephants that this approach outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, we identify potential pitfalls in few-shot learning and propose an unbiased evaluation protocol to mitigate these issues. Experimentation confirms the effectiveness of the proposed method, yielding improvements of 0.2-0.3 F1 points and in some cases 50% fewer parameters needed for the task at hand.

High-definition aerial images possess the unique capability to capture real-world scenes with minimal distortion, thereby serving as an ideal substitute for conventional street-level views. Nevertheless, existing HS photography technology is hindered by slow data capture rates due to the need for synchronized capture across three spectral bands. In this research, we introduce an innovative, weakly-supervised semantic segmentation approach specifically designed for HD aerial images, leveraging a co-registered tricolor HS image simply acquired through a low-frame-rate camera. By integrating a specially devised hyperspectral center loss in our proposed backbone network, we successfully develop a versatile hyperspectral representation capable of accurately encoding objects and predicting segmentation labels despite varying levels of spectral ambiguity. Furthermore, our approach necessitates minimal manual annotation, necessitating only global image segmentation guidance through segmentor networks trained using frequently updated mean intersection over segments. In our experiments, we demonstrate exceptional performance on the Cityscapes dataset, surpassing state-of-the-art model results by a significant 12.3% in pixel accuracy.
