This research explores the various methods employed within the infinitesimal calculus of G.W. Leibniz, comparing them to similar techniques used today within the frameworks of formal dealing with the infinite, formal handling of sigmas and big O, and tropical mathematics. We show that the manipulation of infinitesimals can be seen as a specialized case of tropical mathematics, and that both the use of formal parameters and the handling of big O operations enable a precise translation of Leibnizian calculus. We also highlight how the transition from infinitesimals to limits, and specifically to formal limits, allows for a conservation of equalities, and demonstrate that the conversion from Leibnizian calculus to the modern formal handling of the infinite results in the conservation of a broad range of identities, amounting to a significant portion of known mathematical truths.

Upcoming Interferometric HI intensity mapping experiments are expected to achieve high $k$-space coverage with thousands of antennas at low frequencies, where Earth's rotation introduces significant systematic motions. This motivates the use of interferometric observations, leveraging cross-correlation data to remove random Galactic emissions, without needing to filter out signal. We utilize a linear perturbation theory to analyze the impact of these systematic motions on the power spectrum measurements of the HI emission, a effect minimal at intermediate $k$-values but becoming more significant at both low and high $k$-values. This effect can be mitigated by using higher-order cross-correlations, although these offer limited improvements at low $k$-values. We also evaluate the impact of using a spectroscopic approach to remove thermal noise, which shows that while it minimizes bias at high $k$-values, it introduces notable biases at low $k$-values. These findings suggest that present HI intensity mapping experiments may be slightly biased even with the interference technique. Future HI intensity mapping experiments with more precise beam modeling, improved redshift accuracy, and better noise modeling can reduce this effect, but may still experience some bias.

I reflect on my work at the University of California, Santa Cruz, where I studied operator representations of abstract models describing physical systems with multiple degrees of freedom. In particular, I explored how the properties of a system's independence and infinite size affect its implementability by local operators. I derived new, improved assumptions for the realizability of certain quantum systems in terms of local operators, resolving two outstanding conjectures in the field. These assumptions offer insights into the relationship between independence and the locality of operators, potentially beneficial for future research.

One key limitation of recommender systems is data scarcity resulting in considerable variability. Various approaches have been implemented to optimize the effectiveness of recommender systems utilizing natural language processing, hyper-graph matching, and deep learning. This research integrates context-based and behavior-based methods to mitigate the reliance on data and enhance system robustness. The document context model utilizes natural language processing to extract semantic meanings from item descriptions, focusing on shared characteristics to simulate user preferences. The behavior-based model, incorporating hyper-graph matching, analyzes user behavior and engages in preference learning. The combined system leverages the strengths of both models, with results indicating an enhanced performance of 8.2% and 13.6% improvement over the document context and behavior-based models, respectively.

The Cuntz algebra $\mathcal{B}7$ provides a complete unitary representation of the Artin-Wedderburn theorem, which classifies all possible matrix algebras over the complex numbers up to equivalence in terms of their column space dimensions. A specific type of algebra, denoted $B(\mathbb{C}^7)$, consists of all matrices with 7 complex dimensions. In our research, we demonstrate that the spectral distributions of independent GUE random matrices from $B(\mathbb{C}^7)$ and its companion matrix $\Pi B(\mathbb{C}^7)$ in the first column are distinct in probability. In addition, our findings reveal partial partialness in both the relative commutant of $B(\mathbb{C}^7)$ in a larger matrix algebra and the left relative commutant of $\Pi B(\mathbb{C}^7)$. Our analysis depends heavily on a recent breakthrough from Erdobesy et al. and requires further extension of their result to ensure the openness of type $B$ for our specific matrix algebra $B(\mathbb{C}^7)$.

This paper revisits the problem of controllability and observability in timed systems, specifically focusing on the practical consequences of undeterminable timing in control signals on system outcomes. We propose two new notions of observability that take into account the system's transition dynamics and reward structure, aiming to determine whether the system's behavior can be distinguished based on its execution paths. Unlike prior work, which focused on idealized scenarios, our results focus on realistic scenarios with controls subject to distinct activation and deactivation times. The complexity of deciding these new observability conditions is investigated, showing a counter-intuitive result of decidability via a straightforward algorithm. We further demonstrate the relationship between our observability conditions and established concepts in timed automata, highlighting a long-established open problem.

The decay $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi f_0(980)$ has been found to contribute more significantly than previously estimated, which in turn has important implications for determining the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ mixing ratio. As a result, the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ decay rate can be accurately predicted using isospin symmetry, which yields a value of $3.640 \times 10^4 $ sec$^{-1}$. Moreover, the $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^0 \eta$ and $\bar B_s^0 \to J/\psi \pi^+\ \pi^- $ decays show a notable correlation due to the $a_0(980)-f_0(980)$ blending effect, which needs to be considered for accurate predictions of hadronic $\bar B_s^0$ decays involving scalar mesons.

The GRAVITY gathering camera was designed to facilitate the formation of a pupil slicer and enable the creation of a laser comb per element during the development of the GRAVITY FMC+ project. This camera, comprising four distinct components, was tested to assess the impact of various optical phenomena and device limitations. Our findings indicate that optical instability has a negligible effect on image quality but amplify noise during exposure. This noise, characterized as 'cosine bump noise,' has a fivefold increase when processed through the gathering camera. Our research outlines the necessary adjustments to mitigate this noise and presents data illustrating the improvement of signal-to-noise ratio following correction. This noise suppression method resulted in a fourfold improvement in phase map accuracy and facilitated the attainment of 1.5 milliradians per root hemisphere error.

We examine $k$-Center variants in graphs of reduced doubling and freeway dimension. Our analysis shows that for a specific set of doubling graphs, solving the problem exactly is NP-hard, and we propose an algorithm that achieves a 12-approximation under both measures. For another class of graphs with limited freeway dimension, we improve the previous 60-approximation result, yielding a 6-approximation. Furthermore, we define a new metric that connects freeway dimension and doubling rank, and our results imply that this metric induces a geometric relationship.

In our paper, it's demonstrated that every entire function of a specific type, defined by a differential equation and subject to a particular growth constraint, is essentially a polynomial, specifically a quadratic one, when its derivative differs from another function's derivative, also a polynomial, by a constant. This conclusion holds when the functions in question are not identically equal, whereas a counterexample exists when they are the same. Additionally, it has been proven that a non-constant entire function, when its derivative differs from another function's derivative by a constant, is essentially a polynomial, specifically a quadratic one, provided both functions have the same growth rate. This conclusion is contingent on the functions not being identically equal; otherwise, a counterexample exists when they are the same. Lastly, it has been shown that a non-constant entire function, when its derivative differs from another function's derivative by a constant, is essentially a polynomial, specifically a quadratic one, provided both functions have distinct values.

This paper addresses the challenge of solving polynomial linear systems with potential errors, where the coefficients of each equation are -1 or 1, and an incorrect answer can be given for each equation as "yes" or "no". Our main contribution is an improved algorithm for this problem. Under specific conditions, our algorithm can resolve the system in O(n^(1+delta)) operations for large matrices, where delta is a small positive constant, and it does so with high accuracy, offering two options for this level of performance. In addition to this innovation, we introduce an efficient technique for ending the solving process more quickly. This new approach allows us to solve smaller systems more rapidly. Furthermore, our results include novel bounds on the size of linear systems that can be solved exactly with random answers by analyzing the properties of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes and constructing specific LDPC codes to achieve this goal.

In an experiment with parity symmetry, researchers study the simultaneous emission of electron packages from a few thousand plasma bubbles, created by a femtosecond laser interacting with a gas near critical density. The experiment finds that the overall electric field of the X-ray flux shows symmetry properties at specific frequencies that are related to the Pockels effect and protects the emission from certain polarization states. The project involves complex simulations to explain the results and measures the symmetry-protected emission's properties under different conditions. The experiment's findings provide new insights into the symmetry-protected emission and open the door for increased laser peak power using gas targets.

A unified analytical equation of state for the equilibrium gas phase of pure alkali metals has been derived. This concise equation encompasses the perfect gas model, is applicable to all alkali metals, and accurately predicts their behavior across a broad pressure range (up to $\sim 10^5$~Pa) and temperature range (up to $\sim 3 \cdot 10^3$~K). Based on this equation of state, mathematical expressions for key thermodynamic properties and characteristics have been obtained, thereby substantiating the principle of corresponding states within the group of alkali elements.

In the context of a medium with chiral asymmetry caused by fermion vacuum effects, we examined the vector meson spectrum in a medium with chiral asymmetry caused by fermion vacuum effects. The framework combines an instanton model for QCD's vacuum and a Higgs phenomenon for quark condensations. The model reveals a non-zero quark density in the ground state. Applying a medium-dependent Kaellen function, we derived equations of motion for the vector meson in the ground state and obtained a complex spectrum of vector mesons, including ground and excited states, as a function of medium and mass parameters. The results show significant mass changes in the ground state and excited states in different media and highlight the significance of the mass ratio of vector mesons and rho mesons in different media.

We examine the problem of precisely calculating network diameter in large, complex networks that follow a small-world pattern, but are compromised by malicious entities that can manipulate its components. Under the assumption that at least half of the nodes in the network operate normally and have a solid understanding of its structure, we have developed an algorithm that can accurately estimate the network's diameter with minimal communication overhead and predictable measurement errors. Our tests on various small-world networks as well as a real-world example demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of this algorithm.

In numerical relativity, the Hamiltonian and momentum constraints within the Baumgarten-Nester approach can be solved using a second-order elliptic partial differential equation. However, this equation's rapid convergence brings about numerical issues. We've developed a new method to resolve these problems by leveraging the conformal transverse-trace-free projection's asymptotic behavior and introducing a novel parameter extension. This approach requires only two parameters, making it simpler and more efficient than Baugarten-Nester method, particularly when employing a single Schur parameter. We've tested our method using a range of scenarios, including a plane-transverse-slice metric with both analytic and numerical conformal rescales, and a rotating black hole initial data setup.

The main objective of the JUNO experiment involves a detailed investigation into the neutrino mass ordering by utilizing a large, 20,000-ton liquid-scintillator detector equipped with photomultiplier tubes. Before implementing the final, densely constructed target, the experiment's 20-inch PMTs required individual assessment for light output, sensitivity, and uniformity following a protective mass application. Out of 398 PMTs screened, 198 met the required standards for the final detector's inner layer, including the reconstruction of its quenching characteristics through UV illumination. The final, 20-inch PMTs were then deployed in the JUNO experiment's central detector following an inner layer installation in November 2020.

Predicting time series data that spans across multiple dimensions is a highly adaptable task, with applications in forecasting consumer behavior, estimating energy consumption, and analyzing neural activity patterns. Existing time series models primarily focus on single-dimensional data, disregarding the complexity of multi-dimensional time series. This work introduces a novel time series prediction framework that incorporates spatial and temporal correlations within multi-dimensional data. Our proposed framework is built around an adaptive graph convolutional network, allowing for a dynamic connection between different time series components. By exploiting temporal correlations within a single series, along with relationships between multiple series, our model yields a substantial enhancement in forecasting accuracy for diverse data sets. Furthermore, we highlight the practical significance of our findings by evaluating the predicted outcomes against established evaluation metrics. Our framework is implemented using Python and the PyTorch library, with the source code available on our GitHub repository at https://github.com/phamthang/MDTS/tree/adaptivity/mdts/.

Astronomical observations from ground-based telescopes can be distorted by Earth's atmosphere due to differential dispersion that varies by wavelength. Observations made off-axis, other than directly at the zenith, necessitate the use of Atmospheric Dispersion Correctors. Current designs of these correctors are based on atmospheric models which have yet to be verified through on-site measurements. We've carried out a detailed analysis of atmospheric conditions across different sites and our findings suggest that standard models are insufficient for accurately capturing the unique properties of each location's atmosphere. Our research specifically focuses on the MEO site, Atmospheric Dispersion Models are compared and contrasted, including the NIMT, NPL, AADC, AIC, AFOE, APM, LROE, MEO, MROE sites' reference models, and our own experimental model based on laboratory measurements conducted with a Fabry-Perot etalon.

Recently, pre-trained language models have been used to tackle complex multi-label learning tasks, but when trained end-to-end with multiple instructors, the model's logits become difficult to analyze and understand. To address this issue, we propose a new distillation method called PILE, which uses pairwise predictions from multiple instructors to clarify the model's logits through pairwise comparison and normalization. Our experiments demonstrate that PILE has a straightforward design, outperforms existing distillation methods, and achieves competitive results with model re-training, while providing improved semantic understanding and analysis capabilities.

We propose a novel detection method for ultralight bosonic dark matter, which leverages intensity interferometry to convert weak, scattered signals from direct dark matter detection experiments into a highly sensitive detection system for ultra-light bosonic dark matter. By taking into account the full spectral information from a Michelson-type detector response, our interference-based approach can significantly enhance detection capabilities. We illustrate that with existing technology, it is feasible to reach a sensitivity level of $10^{-17}$ erg^2^ cm^-2 fpa^-1 Hz^-1 Hz^-1 for a 1 meter long interferometer, thus significantly improving the overall sensitivity by three orders of magnitude, thereby facilitating further investigation of various ultralight bosonic dark matter scenarios.

The basis pursuit is a crucial method for solving underdetermined linear equations with sparse solutions.  This paper explores whether the basis pursuit has a unique solution across the real number system and breaks it down into two separate problems: first, we examine the sufficiency of optimality conditions for uniqueness, and, building on that, we investigate the sufficiency of certain conditions for optimality.

P4 has become the standard language for configuring reconfigurable programmable switches, with the V1Model architecture being the most widely used implementation. An open-source compiler for the P4 consortium allows for syntax analysis and translation of P416 programs into hardware-independent code, but a compiler backend to map this code to V1Model switch resources is needed. A freely available compiler backend for P416 programs and V1Model architecture-based switches has been missing until now. Commercial solutions exist but come with restrictive terms, hindering research into new mapping algorithms and custom instruction sets. Our work fills this gap with an open-source compiler backend for the V1Model architecture, utilizing heuristic-based mapping algorithms to optimize P416 programs for different hardware resources. This allows rapid prototyping of different mapping approaches and provides resource usage metrics for comparison.

In numerical simulations involving fluid dynamics, the Raviart-Thomas vectors play a crucial role in solving transport equations, especially when dealing with flowing fluids. Despite the widespread use of finite element methods, numerical errors can arise from different sources, potentially hindering accurate solutions. In this study, we focus on the vector transport equation and aim to improve the accuracy of standard Raviart-Thomas discretisations by combining post-processing techniques. These approaches involve modifying the vector variables to achieve consistent and stable results. To this end, we propose two methods: one for increasing the accuracy of vector variables globally, and another for doing so locally within specific areas. These techniques are applied to both pure advection and advection-diffusion problems, and their performance is demonstrated with a range of test cases involving complex geometries.

Federated learning allows for the collaborative training of machine learning models without compromising sensitive data, however, it falls short in ensuring model fairness and data protection. This study combines the efficiencies of federated learning, differential privacy, and fairness awareness to address these limitations, proposing a framework that accommodates various fairness metrics and adaptive differential privacy budgets. To test the efficacy of this framework, the researchers utilized a publicly available dataset to demonstrate the benefits of a novel algorithm that leverages K-means clustering on aggregated federated data, and achieves both fair regression models and compliant differential privacy. Moreover, the performance evaluations showed significant enhancements in both fairness and differential privacy when applying this adaptive approach, particularly when using fractional fairness metrics and clustering sizes that align with the number of clients.

Researchers analyzed collision data between protons and antiprotons, collected by the Large Hadron Collider at CERN, to search for an excited state of the B-c+ particle. By examining decay patterns into various final states, including electron-positron pairs, a candidate for this excited state was identified at a statistical significance of 5.4 sigma. Further analysis suggests the excited state, referred to as B-c*(2P1/2), has a mass of approximately 6841.6 MeV and a width of around 9.7 MeV.

This study introduces a novel class of continuous Runge-Kutta integrators designed to solve differential equations. These integrators can be seen as a continuous adaptation of classic Runge-Kutta methods, allowing them to tackle equations with non-smooth solutions, making them suitable for stochastic equations as well. The integrators maintain the same key properties as their discrete counterparts, including stability, optimal stability, and asymptotic stability. The research demonstrates that these continuous methods can resolve issues related to the 'chattering' problem, a challenge for discrete methods. The theory is illustrated with a practical application, and performance is compared with existing methods in numerical tests.

When learning deep neural networks using large datasets, the cost of storing and processing this data on a single machine can be extremely high, making it impractical for large-scale training operations. To mitigate this issue, researchers have developed techniques such as distributed training and data parallelization to efficiently train neural networks using multiple machines. Despite these advances, the memory requirements for distributed training remain significant, as each machine needs to store a complete copy of the neural network architecture. This paper proposes a new approach called regional critic training that decouples the size of the neural network from the memory requirements of distributed training. By reducing the width of the neural networks stored on each machine, this method allows for more efficient use of hardware, potentially leading to significant memory savings during model-parallel training operations. To demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, researchers have extensively evaluated regional critic training on various image classification datasets and training schedules, achieving notable memory reductions of up to 85% without compromising model accuracy.

Three-dimensional chaotic scattering has garnered less attention than its two-dimensional counterpart.  A new set of rules for creating Wada basins in three dimensions has been developed, involving the use of non-linear boundary transformations.  It was discovered that weak dissipation significantly enhances Wada basins and facilitates the emergence of multi-Wada basins in three dimensions.  This contrasts with the case of weak dissipation in two-dimensional scattering, where Wada basins are diminished.  Multi-Wada basins in three dimensions exhibit an expansive range and are found in numerous three-dimensional chaotic systems.  Additionally, it was found that weak dissipation does not result in the degradation of ACC rates, and in some cases, greatly improves them.  This study may inspire further research into the effects of weak dissipation in three-dimensional scattering systems.

A theoretical model involving an invisible, flavor-changing scalar field called $\sigma$ is examined, with the added constraint that it must not contribute to the gluon chromomagnetic dipole moment, resulting in a relationship between its interaction with fermions and its mass that it obtains when spontaneously breaking a $U(1)$ symmetry. It is shown that despite having a vast number of interactions with fermions, $\sigma$ has a significantly long lifespan due to a specific set of unstable states with short lifetimes that prevent it from decaying into those particular states. As a result, the standard method of searching for flavor-changing scalar interactions using meson decay modes is inadequate and needs to be modified. It is proposed that instead of solely focusing on these meson decay modes, a global fit should be conducted that incorporates all relevant constraints, including those from lepton flavor mixing experiments, low-energy neutrino experiments, and the properties of rare meson decays as well as lepton collisions, in order to determine the model's applicable parameter space. It is discovered that this extensive search yields a considerably more restricted range for the model's applicable parameter space compared to a search that only focuses on rare meson decays alone. Furthermore, it is found that certain regions of the model's applicable parameter space correspond to the $\sigma$ particle having multiple roles, such as resolving the long-standing discrepancy in the muon $(g-2)$ and potentially exceeding unitarity in the top-quark coupling in the top-quark

Human activity recognition in videos poses a persistent problem in computer vision due to the intricate movements involved, their long-lasting durations, and the challenging occurrences in everyday life, which often involve unpredictable contexts, obscure objectives, and varied execution methods. Existing research has primarily focused on recognizing activities confined to a single location, but new work tackles the more intricate task of detecting activities spread across multiple locations within a video. This is achieved by introducing the Hierarchical Attention Network (HAN), which is comprised of an initial module responsible for identifying the starting frame of an activity, and a sequential detection module designed to identify key frames associated with an activity by learning their distinctive features. In experiments, the proposed HAN surpassed the performance of six state-of-the-art models, including conventional techniques and deep learning-based approaches, on the Montalbano dataset, and successfully detected activities in an unsupervised manner, requiring no manual labeling.

Investigating the thermodynamic properties of Reissner-Nordstr$\ddot{o}$m anti-de Sitter black holes as a function of horizon radius leads to an analysis of the stability of these objects. Our research indicates that when the scalar field's amplitude exceeds a certain threshold, the system undergoing thermodynamic process from its equilibrium state will exhibit a change in the black hole's number, thereby creating a white hole. This study supports the weak version of the cosmic censorship conjecture but also reveals cases where it fails.

This article will examine the origins of stars, covering both the formation process and the results that have come from its study. Key concepts like molecular clouds, protostars, and brown dwarves will be highlighted, along with the sophisticated observational tools and advanced simulation techniques that have aided in understanding this process. The article will also discuss the outstanding questions that remain in the field of stellar formation and the potential for future investigations to further our knowledge.

This paper proposes a new method to estimate uncertainty and relevance metrics, like Shannon entropy and mutual information, using Nested Sampling. Our approach hinges on a conceptual connection between Nested Sampling and a variational Bayesian inference framework. Based on this connection, we can derive a straightforward computational procedure to estimate these metrics. Our method has inherent limitations stemming from the underlying optimization, necessitating frequent evaluations of the likelihood function. To mitigate this, we suggest employing quasi Monte Carlo methods for integrals associated with entropy calculations. The proposed method is simple, easy to implement and adaptable to a broad range of statistical models, as illustrated by our application to Gaussian mixtures, deep Gaussian processes, and a deep energy-based model.

We establish the existence of faintly measured solutions to a general first-order hyperbolic conservation law. Specifically, we consider a conservation law expressed as $\tau_t + (\tau f)_x = 0$ within the space of measures, where $\tau$ is a measure and $f$ is a smooth, Lipschitz-continuous function. Solutions to this equation are defined as objects that satisfy the equation and are characterized by a set of conditions, including continuity in a certain weak sense. 
Assuming that the initial data $\tau_0$ is a non-negative measure with at most finite measure, and that $f$ meets certain requirements including being a Lipschitz-continuous function, we show that a solution to the equation exists for any time $t \geq 0$. This solution has the property that its values are composed of a feeble solution $u$ and a non-negative constant $\alpha$, where $u$ is an absolutely continuous function that meets certain smoothness requirements and is subject to the condition $u_t + (uf)_x = 0$. 
The main contribution of the research is the establishment of a criterion for the continuity of solutions to the equation as they vary with initial conditions. This involves showing the existence of a set of bounded variation solutions for any non-degenerate (i.e. neither too large nor too small) initial data and demonstrating that the solutions to the equation are relatively stable in the sense that small changes in the initial data lead to

Cybersecurity specialists face the daunting task of protecting sensitive data from sophisticated cyberattacks like malware, ransomware, and distributed denial-of-service (DoS) attacks. The scale of cyberattacks is increasing at an alarming rate, with the global average cost rising from $200 per incident in 2004 to a staggering $148,869 per incident in 2021. As the cost of managing and mitigating these attacks continues to soar, securing networks has become a top priority for companies. To combat this issue, a new system called NBcoded has been developed, which utilizes machine learning to identify and categorize network assault types. The research discusses the shortcomings of existing classifiers, including their reliance on specialized experts, limited accuracy on limited data, and resource-intensive computation. To address these issues, NBcoded leverages Naive Bayes and Encoder, which leverages attention-based mechanisms and pre-training on massive datasets to effectively classify network assaults, even with reduced data and on resource-constrained devices. The proposed system's performance is evaluated using the NSL-KIT dataset, which showcases its superior accuracy, faster training time, and reduced model complexity, making it an ideal solution for protecting network systems on resource-limited devices.

Let $G$ be a finite solvable group and let ${\rm James--Hall}(\gamma,G)$ denote the maximum possible number of $G$-equivariant homomorphisms from the representation $1\mid G$. In 1974, James and Hall conjectured that ${\rm James--Hall}(\gamma,G)$ is equal to the greatest common divisor of $\gamma$ and $|G|$. This conjecture has been verified for abelian groups, groups whose Sylow $p$-subgroups have order at most three, and other specific cases. However, a counterexample has also been discovered for each of these particular situations. Nonetheless, further progress has been made for nilpotent groups, and the existing proof for those cases has been simplified. Furthermore, a modified James--Hall function has been defined for non-solvable groups, and it has been demonstrated that this function yields a valid inequality involving the greatest common divisor of $\gamma$ and $|G}$/[G,G].

Animal locomotion plays a significant role in the ecological balance, where organisms require energy and effort to move around to sustain life. This movement has a notable impact on local ecosystems, often triggering self-sustaining processes such as decomposition, sediment transport, and vegetation growth. To analyze these effects, researchers must gain insight into animals' movement patterns at both individual and collective levels. Although existing methods primarily focus on understanding individual movements, they tend to overlook the group dynamics. This study proposes a novel, scalable approach for identifying collective movement patterns in large groups, where animals are captured on video. By employing image processing and machine learning techniques, the researchers developed a computational framework to detect and track individual animals, accurately categorize their movement patterns, and cluster similar animals together. The results reveal diverse movement patterns across various groups, including straight-line movements, arcs, spirals, circles, polygons, and other complex shapes. The approach demonstrates high efficiency, with a detection rate of 98% and a relatively low computational load of 13 Megabytes per second. The proposed method effectively identifies collective movement patterns in large groups, where animals are arranged in a regular pattern, such as lines, circles, squares, and triangles. This approach provides a valuable understanding of the dynamics within large animal groups, where individuals exhibit highly coordinated behavior.

Contemporary power grid optimization techniques are primarily based on classical methods which, being heuristic, often lack robustness and reliability in large-scale grid optimizations. Furthermore, these methods often require extensive computational resources and sometimes provide only partial solutions. In this context, we explore the potential of quantum algorithms, particularly the quantum alternating optimization algorithm, to address various power grid optimization challenges. We devise a novel cost function to facilitate optimization of the power grid's load scheduling and branch flow scheduling. Subsequently, we conduct comprehensive simulations to assess the efficacy of the proposed approach. The results demonstrate that quantum optimization outperforms classical methods in load scheduling and branch flow scheduling, leading to substantial computational savings of up to 297.24x and 176.84x respectively.

Using machine learning, we'll show how to automatically identify fundamental physical laws using experimental data, without human input. A deep neural network is trained to find the most accurate physics prediction for a given set of measurements, and when applied to rest mass data for various particles, it surprisingly reveals a discrepancy in the results obtained from the Standard Model of physics versus those measured experimentally. Notably, we've found that neutrinos have non-zero rest masses, which aligns with observations made by multiple experiments. Our findings also indicate that charged leptons follow a different relationship than expected, according to the Standard Model of physics, showing a discrepancy of about 3 sigma. These results are consistent with what have been discovered in experiments studying the muon anomaly, which have found similar discrepancies of about 4.5 sigma.

This study employs the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider to investigate the presence of hypothetical heavy, charged, long-lived particles in proton-proton collisions amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data collected at 13 TeV energy. The search targets particles with significantly reduced ionization compared to standard $c$-quarks, ranging from 5 to 20 GeV per unit of path length. The study focuses on events containing a singular, high-momentum track and often an opposite-charged track at varying distances from the primary interaction point. It further excludes standard model backgrounds using a likelihood-based method, yielding no significant deviations from predicted values at 95% confidence level. The results constrain the cross-section of $Z_{ll}$ bosons to charged particles with mass for $500~\text{GeV}$ and
 $300~\text{GeV}$ respectively, corresponding to the particle's lifetime
 exceeding 570 fs and 3.5 ns, with electric charges between 4/3 and 2. The study's findings are particularly significant due to the particle's reduced detection by muon triggers, offering detection opportunities for future experiments at higher luminocities and energies.

The development of integrated quantum photonics based on single photons is crucial for the creation of robust and controllable quantum systems for basic research, applications, and future large-scale complexes. We have improved the performance of a leading source, integrating sine-shaped waveguide-based emitters with a 94% reflection efficiency and a 98% loss rate for out-of-plane loss, resulting in an overall 86% efficiency for the entire optical path. This enhanced efficiency has led to a notable reduction in the required energy per photon, achieving a level of 10 fJ per photon for the entire optical process. This significant advancement brings us closer to constructing extensive quantum light platforms integrating photons and qubits on a single chip.

Neutron inelastic scattering is a valuable tool that not only allows for the identification of a glass's vibrational modes near its boson peak, but also provides insight into the overall vibrational structure of the material. Despite the limitations imposed by its lower energy and wavevector resolution compared to those of other methods such as light or x-ray spectroscopies, neutron inelastic scattering offers a number of key benefits, including the ability to study a wider frequency range and spatial correlations, as well as the capability to measure these properties under both thermodynamic and externally controlled conditions. As such, neutron inelastic scattering experiments have played a central role in the investigation of the boson peak and its significance in the physics of disordered systems.

Particle physics is becoming a precise science driven by theoretical predictions, 
essential for analyzing experimental data. Future experiments like the LHC 
require advanced computations with high accuracy, prompting an examination 
of progress in evaluating complex Feynman integrals that underpin these 
predictions. This review highlights recent advancements in this field, 
noting significant advancements but also the challenges still obstructing 
progress towards solutions.

We derive two distinct sum principles relating to eigenchannels of energy deposition in complex systems characterized by unitary evolution. One principle applies to systems where multiple inputs are possible, whereas the other is specifically relevant to single-input scenarios. In addition, we investigate how these sum principles can be violated under conditions of non-Unitary dynamics, such as when caused by absorption within the system. These findings are further exemplified through energy deposition eigenchannels in a case study involving a single-dimensional system with discrete energy levels.

We introduce the far 3-kpc spiral arm, a newly detected spiral limb of the Milky Way, located at a radial velocity of approximately -130 km/s and with a position angle close to 90 degrees. This arm contains the SGR 1739-78 and its associated molecular cloud, as identified by a global molecular cloud complex, a prominent stellar stream, a group of young O stars, and far-infrared emission. Analysis of the star formation rate suggests that the far 3-kpc spiral arm experienced a burst of star formation around 1 billion years ago. This region exhibits a high degree of extinction and warm dust presence, indicating a densely populated, star-forming region. The far 3-kpc spiral arm likely undergoes a star-forming episode triggered by the passing of a bar or a spiral arm. This arm's presence challenges existing galaxy simulation models and suggests that bar-induced starbursts are common in the local universe.

Increasingly, optimization methods are being used to uncover a broad range of solutions. Our comparison between multi-solution optimization using genetic algorithms and approach gradient reveals that both methods can indeed be adapted to produce a large number of optimal solutions. Our analysis also shows that evolutionary methods are more effective at generating diverse solutions, but are less effective at finding the overall best solution, whereas approach gradient excels in this aspect while struggling with solution diversity. To overcome these limitations, we modify approach gradient to incorporate fitness-shaping techniques, allowing it to produce more diverse solutions without sacrificing its ability to find high-quality ones. Our study provides a framework for future research into the properties of multi-optimization methods.

The Stable Roommates problem concerns pairing a set of agents according to their individual preference lists with specific hierarchical rankings. A key condition for any established pairings is that they must remain stable - preventing the situation where two agents would prefer each other over their respective matches. Variants of the Stable Roommates problem, including its three-dimensional form, invite investigation into what can be achieved given varying constraints on agents' preferences. When the form of these preferences is structured in a linear, additively separable manner, the three-dimensional Stable Roommates problem proves to be particularly complex, equivalent in difficulty to solving a combinatorial optimization problem with applications in resource allocation. A key challenge in tackling this problem is that standard techniques used to find stable allocations may not be applicable due to the preferences' structure, rendering even finding a feasible solution a complex problem and one that is provably not solvable using a polynomial-time algorithm.

Our research systematically explores how different mechanisms of electron-phonon coupling influence valley behavior in two-dimensional materials. We found that when multiple mechanisms of electron-phonon coupling are active, their combined effect can be trivially incorporated into the band structure using a constant energy-dependent effective mass. This constant effectively captures the average impact of all active electron-phonon coupling mechanisms. We also demonstrate that the mechanism of kinetic energy transfer through phonons has a significant influence on valley behavior, particularly when there is a substantial difference in valleys. This mechanism typically has a considerable impact on the valley gap, especially when there are significant phonon gaps between the valleys. On the other hand, the mechanism of orbital diffusion via phonons has a relatively minor influence on valley behavior, primarily when there are no phonon gaps between the valleys. Through the analysis of a specific two-dimensional multivalley material, hBN, we reveal how the band structure of the valence bands in high-symmetry valleys is affected under different conditions and at varying temperatures. Our research provides a foundational understanding of the influence of electron-phonon coupling on valley behavior in two-dimensional materials, paving the way for the exploration of novel phenomena in these systems.

In this paper, we define the concept of cloud completeness and develop criteria for completeness in various cloud structures, obtaining essential properties of cloud centers along the way. We demonstrate that completeness in the GH-category of cloud pairs is equivalent to a specific property of clouds having indistinguishable center points, and we characterize the centers of complete clouds.

This research introduces a microstrip patch antenna designed to operate at mm-waves with a broad bandwidth. Built with affordable technology in mind, the antenna is created using microstrip substrates and features a simple, compact design.  The antenna's microstrip patch incorporates multiple slots microstrip patches for mutual coupling, enabling a broad bandwidth of 5.2% operating at 18.15 GHz.  The integration of a slotted ground plane with the microstrip patch facilitates polarization diversity without increasing size or weight.  The antenna exhibits an impressive conical beam pattern due to the integrated slot microstrip patch microbeam radiating element and a slotted ground plane acting as a reflector element.  The antenna's microbeam pattern provides a vast angular range of 100° for both azimuth and elevation angles.  The localization capability of the antenna within the plane or perpendicular to its microstrip patch is also investigated.  The antenna's performance is measured and analyzed in accordance with the requirements set by the IEEE for mm-wave communications.  The measured results demonstrate an 80% minimum power density within the conical beam pattern, encompassing 100° angular range.  The measured results also show an 85% maximum directivity, ranging from 0° to 100° angular range.  The proposed antenna's measured results surpass the IEEE requirements for its microstrip patch directivity.  Specifically, the measured results show an 85% maximum directivity, specifically 6.15 dB when measured

The reliability of quantum computing systems is at risk due to faulty quantum gates. Existing techniques for coping with this issue involve controlling the density of connections between qubits, but this comes with its own set of limitations when implemented through fault-tolerant logical qubits. The administration of logical subspaces via syndactic densities and protective circuits presents an opportunity for the application of reinforcement learning (RL) principles in codeword design, an approach previously unexplored in the field. Our research delves into the utilization of RL coders as a novel means of constructing stabilizer codes capable of withstanding gate errors, including randomized and generalized forms. The resulting coder portfolios include RL-coded quantum surface codes and twisted torical codes that demonstrate enhanced robustness to arbitrary gate errors. Furthermore, our analysis extends to the case of simultaneous gate errors affecting multiple qubits.

Quantum metrology enhances precision by leveraging the principles of quantum physics. This can be accomplished through interferometry, where the phase information is extracted using gradient-like measurements in conjunction with entangled particles. Even in the absence of measurements, phase information can be extracted using quantum entanglement, a phenomenon known as quantum leverage effect, which exceeds classical bounds. This research investigates a two-cavity network to demonstrate quantum leverage effect in optical systems, utilizing entangled states generated through the exchange of photons. The entanglement's utility is further showcased in determining the source phase and frequencies of two lasers, revealing significant improvements in precision beyond the standard Rayleigh criterion. Lastly, we discuss the implications of quantum leverage effect in the field of laser technology.

The PHENIX Collaboration has collected data on direct photon-hadron correlations in 200 GeV/A Au$+$Au, $d$$+$Au, and $p$$+$$p$ collisions from 2006 to 2011. These findings reveal that cold nuclear matter has negligible effects on $d$$+$Au collisions. A notable disparity exists in hadron production between Au$+$Au and $p$$+$$p$ collisions. Hadrons with high momentum fractions are suppressed in Au$+$Au, whereas those with lower momentum fractions show increased yields, exceeding $p$$+$$p$ collisions. This excess, linked to jet-like correlations, persists beyond the range of original jets. This phenomenon is more pronounced at lower hadron $p_T$ and exhibits jet-medium interactions. In order to further investigate this, the EPOS LHC simulation was used to separate contributions from jet-medium interactions and jet-propagation losses. A comparison with theoretical models, including jet-quenching and diffusion models, follows in a separate publication.

To mitigate the limitations of quantum computers lacking fermionic properties, we leverage a hybrid digital-analog approach in quantum computing. This method utilizes fermionic operators in a quantum analog system to represent wave functions, which are then mapped to Fock space via linear transformations involving fermionic basis vectors. Despite the lack of native fermionic qubits, our approach enables the precise emulation of complex fermionic systems, potentially leading to significant advancements in fields like materials science and chemistry through the resolution of difficult many-body problems.

A key challenge in personalized finance lies in developing investment policies that prioritize both optimal returns and broad applicability to various scenarios.  Constructing features from historical wealth data can be a valuable approach to tackle this problem, but the features must be resilient to random fluctuations in the data.  This paper introduces the Wealth feature constructor, which generates features from both historical wealth data and economic indicators to assist in developing universal financial policies.  To validate the effectiveness of the Wealth constructor, the authors employ a range of generalization tests based on multiple game theory metrics to compare different feature construction techniques.  The study demonstrates that Wealth constructor features yield superior generalization performance across multiple metric categories when compared to alternative methods of feature construction.

A novel binary-binary multi-level approach is introduced for designing a feedforward linear control system to produce numerous intricate structures simultaneously within a three-dimensional tissue volume, where the light intensity modulation matrix is controlled by an amplitude-only binary mask fed by an analog signal. The system's rapid convergence and accuracy are enhanced by utilizing the last iteration's control signal in conjunction with a weight matrix tailored for optimal performance, which can be adjusted based on the desired output matrix's singular valve regions. The resulting system is capable of generating intricate patterns and various shapes within tissue, as demonstrated by its ability to produce multiple two-dimensional structures, a three-dimensional lattice, and a rotating Mandelbrot fractal pattern, as well as a volumetric gradient pattern with inherent spatial multiplicity.

We appreciate the discussion opportunity facilitated by editors and valuable input from discussants. Our work is influenced by the inspiring research of Kallus (2020), which enhances policy learning efficiency using centralized capacity limits. Building upon this foundation, we diversify our findings by considering multiple policies and adapt our methods to account for constraints on both the policy and outcome functions. In the context of robust policy learning, we apply our techniques to a variety of models, including those with known and unknown support, and provide analysis under both empirical and empirical Bayes risk frameworks. Discussants bring attention to exciting new perspectives and areas for further exploration, such as the utilization of constrained policy representation, post-processing techniques, and future research on adapting our methods to work with sample splittting and non-parametric estimators.

Monolithic CMOS sensors featuring small collection electrodes are advantageous due to high signal quality and low power consumption. However, these sensors have limited functionality due to the use of thin high-resistivity epitaxial layers during fabrication. In this study, researchers investigate the active sensor depth using the CLICTD technology, a small collection-electrode monolithic demonstrator. Particle beams are utilized to analyze the charge collection properties and device performance across various thicknesses under different beam angles. In CMOS sensors utilizing a high-resistivity Czochralski substrate, a notable enhancement is observed, with the sensitive volume increasing two-fold, subsequently yielding significant gains in detection efficiency and spatial/temporal resolution.

We've successfully tested a fast atmospheric self-coherent camera system on the Santa Cruz Extreme Adaptive Optics Testbed and recorded its first experimental data under diverse conditions. This system incorporates an artificial intelligence-driven image processing algorithm to eliminate remaining turbulence-induced speckles across a telescope's field of view, utilizing fast spatially-resolved data obtained from a laser beacon. We've experimented with different image processing speeds to maintain coherence and observed the effects of image rotation, speckle size, and orientation on the final image quality. We've discovered that our system can maintain high-quality images up to 100-200 times faster than the relevant Taylor frequency, allowing it to effectively utilize fast phase information generated by advanced adaptive optics systems and reduce remaining speckle statistics even further. We've observed improved signal-to-noise ratios of around 5-10 dB in the laboratory tests. With the ability to rapidly eliminate residual speckles, this system significantly enhances ground-based astronomical observations, particularly for high-resolution imaging and polarimetry applications, by improving image quality, reducing rotation angles, and maintaining the full field of view.

This study presents a novel exogenous kernel for the Cox-Ingersoll model, ensuring negative interest rates stay negative, and brings together key elements from the Hanouf-Bonabeau and Bru-Borovikov models. It introduces a mathematical explanation for the kernel's acceptability for negative rates, and combines this kernel with the Cox-Ingersoll model, yielding the deterministic-shift augmented CIR model. Notably, the new model possesses exactly one positive eigenvalue and two non-positive eigenvalues, and its solution exhibits mean-reversion properties, along with positive mean-reversion rates for both the short-rate and a target rate. Furthermore, the model's distribution is calculated using the Karhunen-Loeve expansion, and its likelihood is derived via the Kalman filter; simultaneous estimation of model parameters is achieved via the Broyden-Fletcher-Goldfarb-Shanno method, and two numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the model's performance in generating negative interest rates.

Research into the characteristics of neutrino oscillations using active neutrinos may also lead to discoveries about sterile neutrinos, specifically in their associated parameters. We investigate the potential of DUNE, a forthcoming experiment, in searching for sterile neutrinos with masses in the GeV range. Our findings rely on the formulation of neutrino oscillations via the weak mediators, and assume that neutrino decays and external backgrounds can be negligible. Within this framework, DUNE has the capability to provide low-statistics evidence for anti-neutrino decays into GeV-scale sterile neutrinos, and subsequently, we define the required parameters for this evidence. Additionally, long-term data collection from DUNE has the capability to deliver high-statistics evidence for neutrino decays into lighter sterile neutrinos within certain mass ranges.

When conducting meta-analyses with mixed effects, such as in the case of robust correlation analysis, the assumption of independent samples often doesn't hold. In order to correct this, researchers have developed various bias-correcting estimation methods. This study extends those methods to bivariate mixed effects and provides a new cluster-adjusted estimator. We examine the performance of this estimator in small sample sizes and compare it to existing estimators, including White's, Huber-White's, and Sanderson's. Our analysis also addresses the question of how to properly calculate the standard error in this context.

This study introduces an advanced integration method designed to simulate multiple steps of particle collisions when resolving individual particle movements. Traditional simulation methods struggle with the constraint of only advancing time steps in accordance with collision frequencies, limiting their application to low Reynolds numbers and simple collision models. In response, we've developed a novel approach, demonstrated through numerical modeling, to effectively simulate complex conditions, such as turbulent flows, high Reynolds numbers, and sophisticated collision models, all while maintaining accurate representations of particle collisions.

Investigating the source of radiation energy in the Unruh/Hawking process is necessarily tied to understanding how particles arise from the virtual pairs.  Virtual pairs' emission dynamics are explored using the DGRT method.  Analysis reveals that radiation particles indeed originate from one member of each pair, but due to virtuality, its momentum differs from the emitted photon's.  This leads to a confusion about radiation source identification.  Clarification requires examining particle creation mechanisms beyond the standard quantum field theory framework, specifically within the context of a non-stationary, highly non-equilibrium situation characterized by extreme gravitational fields and high temperatures.  Virtuality's impact on particle emission is a defining feature of this quantum state.

The color dipole formalism's predictions for nuclear modification factors (NDFs) for transverse momentum spectra in the presence of a hot and dense environment, such as that created in ultra-relativistic heavy-ion collisions, have been found to be insufficient. The underlying reason for this discrepancy is the over-estimation of the effect of collective nuclear motion, which in real-world scenarios is counter-intuitive due to the compensating positive and negative fluctuations in different planes of transverse momentum. The color dipole formalism incorporates collective nuclear motion through the use of coherent fluctuations described via Gaussian distributions, with the result that a single rapidity interval is often affected by redundant negative fluctuations in other directions, thereby artificially increasing the nuclear modification factor beyond actual observations. This limitation has been found to be more pronounced at lower values of parton momentum, resulting in the under-estimation of nuclear modification factors for central collisions and the over-estimation of factors for semi-central and peripheral collisions above a certain threshold of centralness. The potential remedies for addressing this issue are discussed.
This article presents whole number solutions for the equation $a^2+ab+b^2=7^n$ when $n$ is greater than or equal to $3$.

When a liquid jet enters a channel filled with a different liquid, the interface between the jet and the surrounding stream creates a shear boundary, generating turbulence and causing the jet to break up into small droplets.  This study uses high-speed imaging to photograph the interaction between the jet and the stream, and then analyzes the resulting images to measure the movement of individual droplets within the jet, revealing that the droplets accelerate as they near the point where the jet meets the stream, and then suddenly decelerate just before entering the stream, resulting in the formation of highly pressurized, satellite droplets on the main droplet's periphery.  This sudden deceleration creates a pressure gradient that causes the formation of the satellite droplets, and the acceleration and deceleration both contribute to the intense disturbance of the jet-stream interface, and therefore the jet's break-up into small droplets.  Additionally, the study finds that the size of the satellite droplets increases as the jet travels further into the stream, and that the size of the droplets also varies according to the jet's velocity, with higher velocities resulting in larger droplets, and therefore more severe break-up of the jet.  This phenomenon is critical in understanding how jets behave when they enter streams, and the researchers suggest that the size of the droplets will affect how the droplets interact with each other, and therefore the shape of the resulting droplet chain, and the size of the droplets will also affect how quickly

High-performance computing systems rely heavily on fault tolerance to prevent data loss and ensure system reliability. Recent advances in non-volatile memory have made it feasible to achieve crash consistency in such systems with minimal performance impact. However, implementing full crash consistency across an entire system is impractical due to its prohibitively high cost. To address this issue, we introduce a novel approach, called NVMcheck, which strikes a balance between achieving crash consistency and maintaining minimal performance impact for HPC applications. NVMcheck leverages check-pointing to isolate and correct errors within individual tasks, thereby extending the concept of crash consistency to entire systems. The approach involves introducing runtime algorithms that monitor memory access and create check-points before each synchronization event, along with a data structure to track modified data and perform error correction. We implemented NVMcheck across multiple compilers and evaluated its effectiveness on real-world applications, which showed that it achieves sub-millisecond check-pointing intervals and allows for precise error isolation with minimal performance impact. The approach also enables developers to select from various error handling strategies, including roll-back, data recovery, and task termination, which in turn facilitates the optimization of performance overhead. We also conducted micro-benchmarks to validate the feasibility of using finite machines in the recovery process and demonstrated that our approach outperforms existing crash recovery methods by executing check-pointing twice during each iteration of a critical section.

Organizational frameworks like knowledge graphs, product categorizations, and document taxonomies use hierarchical relationships to simplify complex associations and improve related item recommendations. Existing hierarchical structures can also inform machine learning models, enhancing their performance. Despite their importance, these frameworks are often constructed manually or using outdated methods, incapable of adapting to modern big data. To address this, researchers have developed new approaches to create these frameworks, which we will introduce in this study. Our comparison of these methods in real-world scenarios reveals that they struggle with scalability, often failing to handle datasets larger than 10 million entities. In response, we develop three scalable frameworks, able to create these frameworks for billions of entities. Our results show that, when applied to the knowledge graph, our approaches outperform the current best methods, reducing computation time by an impressive 18 times for hierarchical relationships and 96 times for semantic grouping.

We conducted an exhaustive examination comparing the statistical properties of non-hierarchical three-body systems with corresponding theoretical models. By running millions of simulations based on a variety of initial conditions, we measured distribution patterns for quantities like energy, angular momentum, and collision rates. These statistical measurements were then compared to two predictive models derived by E. Giltug and S. McLaughlin, specifically considering the impact of final binary collision properties and parabolic escape velocities. Following this, we ran millions more simulations to assess predictions related to final binary interaction types, ranging from grazing to catastrophic collisions. Ultimately, these results validate the predictions made by McLaughlin, offering a statistical foundation for a newly developed theoretical framework, and provide a practical tool for forecasting the future evolution of gravitational three-body systems.

Data from $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV pp collisions and $\sqrt{s_{\rm NN}}=5.02$ TeV PbPb collisions collected by the LHCb detector are used to determine the suppression ratio of $J/\psi$ and $\psi(2S)$ production in 0--8.9 $m_{\rm T}$ and 0--1.6 $m_{\rm T}$ $p$-TeV intervals, respectively. The measured values are 0.62 $\pm$ 0.06 + 0.03 $-$ 0.04 (stat) $\pm$ 0.03 (syst) for $J/\psi$ and 0.84 $\pm$ 0.06 $\pm$ 0.03 (stat) $\pm$ 0.06 (syst) for $\psi(2S)$, when compared to their corresponding pp collision results. The measured levels of suppression are 0.18 $\pm$ 0.04 (stat) $\pm$ 0.03 (syst) for $J/\psi$ and 0.20 $\pm$ 0.07 $\pm$ 0.03 (stat) $\pm$ 0.06 (syst) for $\psi(2S)$, in 8--20 $m_{\rm T}$ $p$-TeV intervals.
